detail.abstract: Every Federal Reserve announcement carries three surprises: a change in the expected policy path, a revision of the central bank's assessment of the economy, and the tone of the statement. We identify them as mutually orthogonal shocks on 219 announcements from 1994 to 2023, combining the Jarociński and Karadi (2020) sign-restriction decomposition, the Bauer and Swanson (2023b) orthogonalisation on the pre-announcement macro state and a Transformer classifier fine-tuned on the Shah et al. (2023) corpus, and trace each to the CRSP/Compustat cross-section, which is free of survivorship bias. The rate-path surprise dominates: a one-standard-deviation hawkish surprise lowers the market by about half a per cent, with the same sign in every regime and in nearly every rolling window, with a surprise built without equity prices, and on the announcements of 2024-2025. Its cross-section is the arithmetic of market exposure: the return to beta is what the CAPM implies from the market move, size adds little, and the balance-sheet characteristics that the literature associates with monetary transmission carry their usual signs on their own but none survives beta and size, in linear projections or in causal forests evaluated out of fold. The information surprise is small and positive. The tone surprise is small on average and its sign differs across periods, a pattern that bootstrapping the construction of the surprise, the level of the policy rate, the press conference and the announcements of 2024-2025 fail to confirm. Pre-registered predictions for 2024-2026 are reported as rejected, with a dated ledger of every deviation from the plan.

title: Temperature and Chronic Hunger: A Nonlinear, Distributed-lag Panel Estimation of the Climate-undernourishment Relationship in 133 Countries, and Why Cross-Country Emissions Effects Reflect Common Trends
affiliations: Kathmandu University - Kathmandu University School of Management

detail.title: Temperature and Chronic Hunger: A Nonlinear, Distributed-lag Panel Estimation of the Climate-undernourishment Relationship in 133 Countries, and Why Cross-Country Emissions Effects Reflect Common Trends

detail.abstract:
The macroeconomic climate literature identifies temperature effects on output growth
from within-country weather variation, and the agronomic literature documents
nonlinear temperature effects on crop yields and total factor productivity. Yet the
chronic-hunger indicator that anchors Sustainable Development Goal 2 - the FAO
prevalence of undernourishment (PoU) - has rarely been the object of a global panel
that models climatic nonlinearity, allows for delayed effects, and is robust to the
common global trends that pervade cross-country climate data. This paper fills that gap
using a near-balanced panel of 133 countries over 2000-2021. Identifying climate
effects from year-to-year within-country temperature anomalies in a two-way (country
and year) fixed-effects framework with distributed lags and Driscoll-Kraay standard
errors, I find that temperature exerts a robust, concave, and delayed effect on
undernourishment: the response accumulates over one- to two-year lags, and the
cumulative within-country effect is economically meaningful. A central methodological
result is that the positive association between greenhouse-gas emissions and
undernourishment - visible in specifications without common time effects - disappears
once year effects are absorbed, indicating a spurious global co-trend rather than a
country-level channel; this speaks directly to the ongoing debate over trend controls in
climate econometrics. Precipitation carries no robust effect, echoing the macro-panel
literature. An exploratory Hansen (1999) threshold model detects a rural-population
regime split. Still, because the rural share is overwhelmingly cross-sectional, it is
interpreted as a structural-development gradient rather than a within-country amplifier.
The contribution is a credibly identified, nonlinear and lagged temperature-damage
function for chronic hunger, together with a cautionary demonstration that emissions
effects in global food-security panels are artefacts of common trends.

detail.abstract: The recent introduction of the one-day volatility index (VIX1D) by the Chicago Board Options Exchange reveals a persistently positive short-term volatility risk premium (VRP). This empirical finding underscores the importance of pricing short-term volatility risk and challenges Generalized Auto-Regressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (GARCH) models, which imply a zero one-day VRP under the local risk-neutral valuation relationship (LRNVR). Motivated by this inconsistency, we propose a hybrid VIX1Dimplied stochastic volatility-in-mean (VSVM) model to demonstrate that the LRNVR assumption does not hold under a stochastic volatility framework, enabling the VSVM model to better capture the dynamics of the one-day VRP.

detail.abstract: In India between 2010-11 and 2024-25, the price a private college charged rose at 10.2 per cent a year while the pay a new graduate earned rose at 2.6 per cent and fell by 30.3 per cent in real terms. In ordinary markets, when a good becomes more common its price falls. Here the opposite happened: the number of degree-holders grew by 38.5 per cent, the number of institutions by 31.9 per cent, the gross enrolment ratio from 21.1 to 30 per cent-and fees doubled in real terms. This paper names that contradiction the Double Inflation Principle: a market failure in which credential devaluation accelerates tuition inflation through an escalating positional arms race. On a new 15-year panel of 50 named private colleges-every 2024-25 fee published, six fee histories published, the remaining paths reconstructed and used only as a validated simulation device-every hypothesis is tested on published data alone. Reputation band and stream explain 84.5 per cent of the variation in observed fee levels; across eight published fee histories the wedge over the cost floor rises with positioning intensity (exact permutation p = 0.053); the premium segment compounded 115 per cent of excess price over the cost of running itself, and that credential value per rupee fell to 63-78 at the top of the market. A value equation closes the loop: every rupee of excess price is, by arithmetic, a rupee of value destroyed, which pushes the next cohort upmarket-CAT registrations rose 61.3 per cent-where the sellers of the better signal raise their price. I prove the loop's fixed point, estimate its gain, and report every null result honestly.

detail.abstract: This paper examines gender differences in competitive preferences among university students in Delhi NCR using an incentivised experiment adapted from Niederle and Vesterlund (2007) across 14 colleges, with 255 participants, equally balanced by gender and academic background. Participants complete arithmetic tasks under piece-rate and tournament compensation schemes and are subsequently given a choice between them, alongside measurement of self-confidence through elicitation of belief about relative ability and their risk preferences. Consistent with existing literature, we observe a substantial gender gap in tournament entry: 44.5 percent of men choose the tournament scheme compared to 20.5 percent of women. Beliefs account for a large share of the gap and remain a strong predictor of competitive entry across both contexts. However, even after controlling for beliefs, performance, and risk preferences, a residual gender difference persists. This gap is strongly contextdependent as it only arises in forward-looking decisions under uncertainty, not when choices are based on realised performance. We further find that women place less weight on positive performance signals when forming these beliefs, contributing to lower competitive entry. This effect is strongest among high-performing women, for whom the cost of non-entry is highest. These findings suggest that closing the gender gap in competitiveness requires addressing belief formation rather than preferences alone.

detail.abstract: This paper provides an analytical model to study the effects of pre-release policies such as amnesties and pardons on crime rates and cooperative behavior in a population by using a game theoretical framework. A crime is defined as a violation of social norms and is punished when detected. In our model, prosocial, cooperative behavior is considered the norm of society. In this sense, acting selfishly at the expense of society will constitute a crime that can be punished with a sanction upon detection. We are using the hawk-dove game to capture the choice between prosocial (altruism and cooperation) and antisocial behavior (selfishness). Firstly, the dynamics of the model are studied without amnesty; then, we implement amnesty into our model, and finally, we analyze the effect of pardon by using an agent-based model since pardon requires information about agents' crime history. We find that amnesty not only reduces the effectiveness of sanctions but also makes more agent criminals since the cost of crime is lower even if the payoff is not strictly better than before.

detail.abstract: Faults are the principal impediment to achieving high levels of efficiency, reliability, and longevity in photovoltaic (PV) systems. In this article, we systematically reviewed solar PV fault diagnostics techniques and compared different fault signature interpretations based on three primary data sources: electrical measurements, environmental conditions, and thermal inspection images. We have evaluated five basic approaches; (i) Electrical Approaches; (ii) Thermal Approaches; (iii) Statistical Approaches; (iv) Optimization-Based Methods; (v) Machine Learning Techniques. relative to their diagnostic evidence, measurement requirements, fault coverage, and specific fault categories and along with several operational parameters including System Topology, Localization Scope, Validation Conditions, Acquisition Intervals. Overall, our evaluation shows there is no single optimal method for identifying faults of all types, primarily because of differences in datasets, definitions of faults, validation conditions and timing measures which make it difficult to make direct comparisons. Finally, we identify possible areas for future research; Hybrid Physical/Data-Driven Models, Digital Twins, Embedded Inference, Standardized Datasets, Learning with Limited Labels, Longitudinal Field Evaluations.

detail.abstract: Monetary incentives for public goods provision do not necessarily enhance efficiency, while baseline willingness to contribute remains anchored to risk-neutral expectations. detail.abstract: This paper studies the relative wage distortion and income inequality between high and lowskilled workers, comparing exporters and non-exporters in China. We develop a model featuring heterogeneity in firm productivity, worker skills, and firms' export decisions. By estimating relative wages and relative marginal productivity, we construct a new indicator that measures relative wage distortion between high-and low-skilled workers and contrast it with income inequality. Using data from Industrial Firms and Customs, we construct instrumental variables with tariffs based on China's accession to the WTO and the reform of trading rights in China. We find empirical evidence that is consistent with the model predictions: on average, Chinese exporters have higher wage inequality but lower relative wage distortion than non-exporters. This is driven by ordinary trade firms, and we observe lower wage inequality but higher relative wage distortion among processing trade firms. We also carry out heterogeneity analysis based on firm ownership, existence of labor unions, and regional market differences.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the macroeconomic effects of attacks on oil tankers. We identify oil-shipping-cost shocks by combining a narrative record of attacks on oil tankers along key routes in the Middle East and Southeast Asia with high-frequency changes in tanker freight rates. Focusing on the period following the U.S. shale expansion, we find that these shocks lower economic activity and raise consumer prices in both the United States and the world economy. These responses differ from those associated with conventional oil supply shocks and disruptions to dry-bulk shipping. Especially, crude production and oil prices show no significant immediate response, while inventories decline. Moreover, U.S. evidence points to an energy-trade channel, with increased congestion at Middle Eastern ports, lower crude imports and refinery inputs, leading to higher fuel prices. We also document that manufacturing orders and shipments fall immediately, consistent with precautionary adjustments in firms' purchases and investment plans. These findings, together with the contraction in global activity, suggest that oil-shipping disruptions can hurt both oil-importing and oil-exporting economies.

detail.abstract: Pollination is a central ecosystem service for agricultural production, but most macroeconomic models still treat pollinator decline as a generic productivity shock. This paper develops a static computable general equilibrium (CGE) framework that explicitly represents pollination services as a primary production factor within an extended Bio-Social Accounting Matrix. The model is calibrated separately for France and Italy using 2015 BioSAM data, and pollinationservice shares are derived from crop-specific dependence coefficients aggregated to the model's sectoral structure. Simulations examine moderate and severe declines in pollination effectiveness, together with two mitigation options: targeted production support and ecosystem restoration. Results show that a 10% decline produces limited economy-wide effects, while a 30% decline generates substantial contraction in highly dependent agricultural activities and spreads to household consumption, investment demand, trade flows and factor returns. Italy shows stronger household and investment losses, reflecting its exposure to Mediterranean horticulture and permanent crops, whereas France shows larger external-balance adjustment under the fixed-exchange-rate closure. Policy results indicate that activity subsidies only partly cushion selected sectors and can worsen fiscal and macroeconomic pressures because they do not restore the ecological input itself. By contrast, restoration that partially recovers pollination effectiveness sharply reduces production, consumption, investment and trade losses. The findings demonstrate the value of integrating ecosystem-service inputs directly into economywide models and support pollinator conservation and restoration as macroeconomically relevant components of agri-food resilience.

detail.abstract: Physical intelligence refers to intelligence systems that understand, reason about, and act in accordance with the physical world and its underlying laws, dynamics, and constraints. Unlike conventional AI systems, physical intelligence interacts continuously with uncertain physical environments, and its actions produce consequences that are physically irreversible. As existing trustworthy AI frameworks have been developed primarily for digital AI systems, they do not fully capture the distinctive challenges of Physical Intelligence, such as physical safety, cyber-physical security, and physical manufacturing process. To address this gap, we present a survey of trustworthy physical intelligence principles. First, we characterize the core capabilities and challenges of physical intelligence. Second, we examine the role of physics in AI. Third, we trace the end-to-end physical intelligence life cycle across five core stages and introduce Trustworthy Physical Intelligence Operationalization (T-PAIO). Fourth, we develop the Trustworthy Physical Intelligence (T-PAI) framework, a theoretical framework that organizes key trustworthiness principles and provides a foundation for governing trustworthy physical intelligence systems.

detail.abstract:
Modern finance has become extraordinarily good at moving payment instructions while leaving the deeper mechanics of settlement largely invisible to end users. A card transaction can be authorised in seconds, a bank balance can be updated instantly, and a transfer can appear complete long before the underlying obligations between institutions are finally settled. GoldTech Ecosystem begins from a different premise: payment and settlement are related, but they are not the same event. Payment concerns the movement of instructions and claims. Settlement concerns the final change in ownership or discharge of an obligation.

This paper sets out an architecture for physical-asset settlement in which the physical asset, the legal and ownership record, the technology layer, and the productive resource layer are treated as distinct but coordinated components. Gold is the principal reference asset because it combines physical scarcity, global recognition, deep market infrastructure and a long history as a monetary asset. The architecture, however, is not defined by a token, public blockchain, card network or bank account. Technology records, authenticates and scales the system; it does not manufacture the underlying asset or substitute for the legal meaning of ownership.

The central proposition is simple: a monetary asset becomes operational only when it can be used to settle economic activity with clear ownership, verifiable backing and defined finality. Holding gold is one problem. Making gold spendable is another. Making gold itself the settlement asset is a different architectural problem altogether. GoldTech Ecosystem is designed around that distinction.

detail.abstract: The U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) arts and cultural production satellite accounts are widely used to measure arts and cultural economic activity nationwide and for individual states. The BEA satellite accounts, however, are not available for regions smaller than states. This research report evaluates four different data sources used to construct 14 alternative measures of arts and cultural activity. These data sources vary in how closely their definitions of arts and culture align with the BEA satellite accounts. Generally, the alternative measures are more highly correlated with BEA “core” arts and cultural activities than with “supporting” arts and cultural activities. Another limitation of the alternative measures is the suppression of industry and occupational employment data for smaller regions (e.g., small counties). The microdata files from IPUMS USA offer an alternative measure of arts and cultural employment that is not subject to data disclosure limitations and is available for regions (i.e., PUMAs) smaller than a state, albeit not counties. Analysis of these data shows that the top 20 areas by arts and cultural employment share are neighborhoods in either New York City or Los Angeles. The analysis also reveals sizable differences in arts and cultural employment shares between metropolitan areas and nonmetropolitan regions. The top five states (including the District of Columbia) are the District of Columbia, New York, California, New Jersey, and Colorado.

detail.abstract: Throughout history, rulers have needed large numbers of people to work, pay taxes and enforce orders. That need is what made them bargain with, feed and fear their populations. If AI and robots can do nearly all productive and military work, the need may disappear. This paper asks what protects people once it does. We built a game-theoretic Monte Carlo simulation of six world blocs from 2026 to 2075 that tracks AI capability and robot build-out, the loss of the public's economic and military leverage, democratic erosion, purges inside ruling groups, and the choices those groups make once their populations are no longer needed. It draws on historical base rates, includes four restraints on rulers found by a historical search with rules fixed in advance, and is cross-checked against a pre-specified elicitation from a judgment model. Like war games and socioeconomic climate scenarios, it compares futures rather than predicting them. Main findings: (1) losing leverage removes the public's protection and nothing structural replaces it; by 2075 the US or China public is disempowered in 94% of runs; (2) the outcome then rests on the restraint and incentives of a few people; (3) the result does not hinge on how closure is reached, though faster AI progress raises the risk; (4) an economic network outside state and corporate control that pays its output to households makes it almost free for rulers to keep people alive: at 50% of US-bloc activity by the early 2030s it cuts the risk of near-total depopulation by more than a quarter, while arriving in 2040 loses about 40% of that effect. Under the stated assumptions, the probability of a deliberate loss of 10% or more of the US or China bloc's population by 2075 is about 0.44, and of near-total loss about 0.38. These numbers show where the assumptions lead, not a forecast.

detail.abstract:
People's basic subsistence needs should not lose their claim to a response because they lack money. The term refers to the needs addressed by basic provision (Paper 2) and shared basic provision (Paper 3). Money can serve exchange and accounting, but it is not an adequate sole means of representing or evaluating basic subsistence needs. Taking food production and access as its principal examples, this paper distinguishes human needs, market demand backed by purchasing power, and the conditions through which needs are actually met. It examines mismatches at both the production and the need-fulfillment stages: when production is organized around income and returns, necessary needs may fail to generate corresponding supply signals; once resources have been produced, people may still be unable to obtain them because they lack purchasing power or the conditions for delivery. In evaluating producers' circumstances, the paper distinguishes industry-level labor inputs, personal income, and autonomous time, without inferring individual leisure from changes in aggregate working hours. Monetary balances can be carried forward, but goods have storage limits, basic needs require timely responses, and human life and labor time cannot be postponed indefinitely. Care, child-rearing, and long working hours further show that monetary compensation does not automatically correspond to the importance of the labor that sustains life. The paper argues that basic provision should be evaluated by people's needs and their actual fulfillment, rather than by ability to pay. This is a normative argument; it does not predetermine an alternative to money or a particular system of provision.

detail.abstract: This paper argues that the world has entered a regime of structurally higher inflation driven by three mutually reinforcing forces: (i) a reserve-currency hegemon whose public debt now exceeds $40 trillion and is cheapest to service by eroding its real value; (ii) the largest private capital-formation wave since the railways, the AI build-out, which spends roughly $700 billion a year in 2026 on physically scarce inputs; and (iii) a US-China rivalry that turns that spending into a matter of state will rather than market return. The well-known part of the story is that fiat money loses purchasing power over time. The new contribution is the AI Capital Deepening Shock: front-loaded AI investment creates demand today and supply only later, and it collides with inelastic inputs (electricity, memory chips, copper, electricians). Because geopolitics makes this spending priceinsensitive, it raises the inflation floor rather than producing a one-off spike. We formalize the argument in a simple debt-dynamics framework, present evidence from official and market sources, and draw one central implication: in this regime, idle cash is the asset most certain to lose, while productive real assets in the hegemon and its allies are the default store of value. We close with the counterarguments that could falsify the thesis.

detail.abstract: The private equity (PE) market is characterized by buyout transactions, in which PE firms acquire the full equity of private companies through highly leveraged positions. This paper examines how the credit market conditions influence PE market performance, and evaluates the impact of PE shock on the United States macroeconomy. We employ two structural vector autoregressions (SVARs), identified by short-and long-run recursive restrictions, to estimate a U.S. sample of Real GDP, Tobin's Q, inside money, credit spread, and the internal rate of return (IRR) of leveraged buyouts (LBOs) from 1986Q1 to 2025Q1. In addition, we estimate a proxy-VAR to identify the PE shock and trace its effects on the macroeconomy. We find that the PE market is sensitive to disturbances from the credit market and the aggregate production sector. The total factor productivity (TFP), credit supply, credit demand, and risk premium shocks generate statistically significant movements in the IRR of LBOs. In contrast, the PE shock does not transmit meaningfully to the real economy at business cycle horizons. It produces no statistically significant responses in real GDP, Tobin's Q, inside money, or the credit spread under either recursive identification scheme or under a proxy-VAR that identifies the PE shock with an external instrument. This result counters what many market commentators' worry that the PE market is a potential source of systemic risk to the U.S. economy.

detail.abstract: Children increasingly encounter artificial intelligence directly through digital services and indirectly through health, welfare, education-linked, safeguarding, benefits, and public-administration systems. Yet governance often treats children principally as vulnerable users, data subjects, or future beneficiaries rather than as present rights holders whose dignity, safety, privacy, equality, development, participation, health, and access to remedy must shape institutional decisions now. This article introduces CHILDRIGHTS AI, a purpose-built, human-governed, AI-enabled present-rights assurance and institutionalaccountability framework for artificial intelligence that directly or indirectly affects children. Methodologically, the article applies a present-rights assurance method integrating doctrinal child-rights analysis, comparative global policy mapping, theory synthesis, sociotechnical safety analysis, implementation-science reasoning, and design-oriented normative framework development. CHILDRIGHTS AI translates six theoretical foundations into eight separately reported assurance domains and a five-part Rights–Duties–Evidence–Voice–Response test. It distinguishes rights-threatening use, conditionally governable use, and use that remains not assessable because evidence is insufficient. The article maps the framework against the Convention on the Rights of the Child, General Comment No. 25, the 2026 Joint Statement on Artificial Intelligence and the Rights of the Child, UNICEF guidance, WHO health-AI guidance, UNESCO’s AI ethics recommendation, the Council of Europe AI Convention, OECD principles, the EU AI Act and GDPR, UK children’s data-protection rules, US sectoral governance, Canada’s automated-decision regime, representative Australian frameworks, and the African Union strategy. It also separates identity or age assurance, rights protection, AI content generation, and final consequential authority. A companion validation protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework on 3 October 2026 and is presently under embargo; this article states the research direction without disclosing the protocol’s restricted instruments or detailed procedures. Subject to validation, a separate confidential technical implementation paper provides the protected engineering and governance blueprint for possible later operationalisation of CHILD-RIGHTS AI as a modular hybrid assurance platform. That paper is withheld, and no operational platform is claimed. The contribution is an original route from children’s present rights to institutional assurance, meaningful participation, accountable decision-making, accessible remedy, and demonstrable governance across the AI lifecycle.

detail.abstract: We model investors with recursive preferences who disagree about real productivity and extraneous risks in a production economy with piecewise linear convex adjustment costs. The discontinuous marginal adjustment costs, jointly with disagreement, result in shifts between the "smooth" and "sticky" equilibrium investment phases. Speculation in financial markets, especially on extraneous risk, can decrease or increase real investment and asset prices depending on whether investors' EIS is less than or greater than 1. Speculation on extraneous risk increases asset (consumption/investment) volatility when equilibrium investment policy is "sticky" ("smooth"). Quantitative studies show that disagreement over extraneous risk can explain variations in aggregate investment, valuation, and volatility of the S&P 500 index, and that model measures of sentiment and disagreement dispersion are highly correlated with their empirical counterparts.

detail.abstract: Background: Local decisions to scale down outbreak response are often informed by periods without new reported cases, yet how often such quiet periods are followed by renewed reporting during an active Ebola outbreak has rarely been quantified. Methods: We analysed 2,233 health-zone-report observations from 60 affected health zones in the 2026 Bundibugyo virus disease outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (15 June-31 August 2026). A monotone cumulative reporting frontier prevented downward data revisions from creating false recurrence. Reported silence was defined as 7, 14 or 21 days without a frontier increase. Results: A 14-day silence occurred in 32 zones; 22 (68.8%, 95% CI 51.4-82.0) later exceeded their previous cumulative maximum, after a median of 12.5 days. Renewed growth followed 7-Preprint-not peer reviewed. Version of October 2026. 1 day silence in 31/41 zones and 21-day silence in 12/21, and was not associated with prior burden. Among newly affected zones with 14 days of follow-up, 4/24 had reached 10 reported cases. Conclusions: Short local reporting plateaus are provisional surveillance states, not evidence that transmission has been interrupted. Response readiness should be maintained through quiet periods, and outbreak dashboards should track time since the last increase rather than binary affected status.

detail.abstract: Do women-owned firms face the same binding constraints as men-owned firms, or a different portfolio? Using nationally representative data on 491,923 proprietary establishments in India's informal sector, we address this question, bridging the growth-diagnostics literature, which studies the full menu of constraints but ignores gender, and the gender-finance literature, which studies gender but only through credit. We find, first, a salience gap: conditional on observables, female proprietors are 2.6 percentage points less likely to report any operational problem, a gap that is larger for long-surviving firms. Second, women and men report non-recovery of financial dues at equal rates, but women citing dues run higherperforming firms-robust to instrumenting-indicating this demand-side friction taxes precisely the women-owned firms scaled into supply chains. Third, a quantity-rationing gap: reporting credit as the most severe problem predicts formal borrowing equally for women and men, but the additional informal borrowing it predicts for men does not materialize for women; among borrowers, women receive 35-44% smaller loans regardless of reported constraints, with no interest-rate difference. Firm scale and maturity moderate the credit gap, caste and urban location the dues gap. Policy should extend beyond credit access to contract enforcement and payment infrastructure.

detail.abstract: We study the geometry of near-singular order-book matrices in the 2 × 2 case. For a 2 × 2 matrix whose four entries are drawn uniformly from the probability simplex, the determinant factorizes as x(1-x)(p-q), and its density at zero is exactly 6. Under a symmetric Dirichlet(α) prior, the density at zero is finite if and only if α > 1/2, with a logarithmic divergence at the threshold and a power-law divergence below it. We identify the normalized matrix with a 2 × 2 contingency table, in which the determinant is the numerator of the phi coefficient and near-singularity is equivalent to statistical independence. We formalize the numerical null space of a near-singular matrix via the singular value decomposition, giving a threshold-free definition of the near-singular state and a scale-invariant measure of the distance to degeneracy. We then test whether the numerical null space direction predicts future relative returns of BTC and ETH. Using two independent datasets-a targeted recording of near-singular events and a full week of sequence-verified level-2 depth from Binance Spotwe find no economically meaningful out-of-sample predictive power for the numerical null direction at horizons from 1 s to 5 min. The one feature with positive out-of-sample R 2 , cross-asset order-book imbalance divergence, contributes R 2 oos = 0.0008, which is positive but negligible. The numerical null space is a well-defined geometric object that does not carry directional, volatility, or correlation information in the data examined. We state the n-asset generalization as an open problem and discuss what would constitute evidence for predictive content in near-singular order books.

detail.abstract: We scored 198 countries and territories (all 193 UN member states, plus Greenland, Kosovo, Palestine, Taiwan and Vatican City) from 0 to 100 on one question: does a person get to see, control and share their own health record? Eight weighted categories cover access to the full record, control and consent, privacy and security, protection from commercial use, a connected care journey, clinician access at the point of care, research consent, and clinical AI governance. Research agents built on Anthropic's Claude models did the research and scoring against a written rubric, and the authors ruled on every finding and every change for the countries; Section 11.7 sets out how rulings were made for the US state layer. The rubric requires an agent to open every source it cites; a later check of every cited link found 7156 cited links checked: 7011 opened, 0 dead (HTTP 404 or 410), 88 blocked by bot protection and 57 unreachable, unresolved or answering with a server error. Every score cites the public pages it rests on: 5147 cited sources (979 undated). Finland (71), Denmark (70), Estonia (68), Hungary (68) and Sweden (67) have the highest scores; allowing for scoring error, each of them is first, alone or tied, in at least 5% of draws. The median is 39, and scores track national income closely: Spearman +0.72 (95% interval +0.64 to +0.79, n 188). By band, with the range each count takes when weights and scores are varied: 9 Strong (7 to 14 across draws), 66 Mixed (58 to 72), 111 Weak (101 to 115) and 12 Poor (10 to 19). No country reaches the top band in any draw; 12 countries are Poor as published (10 to 19 across draws). A blind re-scoring of 58 sampled cells from the first 65 countries by a separate session of the same model family, run before the 2 October re-research, agreed with the scores at that time at an intraclass correlation of 0.82, and a second, of 108 cells from the 133 countries added on 2 October 2026, at 0.84, though single access scores there agree less well (0.68); no human rater has scored the index. A single cell can move by about 17 points. Once a country's scoring error and the weights are both allowed for, a country's likely rank typically spans 43 places. Confidence labels are computed from each country file by a fixed rule: 27 high, 105 medium and 66 low. We also classed where control over the record sits by default, which we call who holds the keys: 51 Shared, 81 Institutional and 66 State; 0 Individual. No country gives the person the default say over who sees the record; our definition of that class requires that nothing flow into a state or provider system by default, which no national system does. An audit of our own scores found that the same legal situation was sometimes scored differently in different regions. We tightened the rubric, rescored, and report every change. A separate context layer, which changes no score, asks whether strained public systems push care to private providers whose records do not reach the public record. Alongside the scores we collected 463 published accounts of real problems with health records. They illustrate the scores and do not change them. Version 1.1 adds a layer for the United States: what the law of each of the 50 states, and of Washington, DC, adds to federal law for a person's health record, on six legal dimensions and four kinds of sensitive record. It gives no state score and no state rank, and it changes no country score. A blind re-reading of 150 sampled cells, by agent sessions that could read only stored copies of the cited pages, agreed with the published cells at an intraclass correlation of 0.965 on the 114 cells with ordered levels where the rater settled a level (a bootstrap interval clustered by state runs from 0.92 to 1.00). Other sessions that searched on their own reported a law the research sessions had not found in 4 of 25 sampled cells, which set off a second search for missed laws. The paper and data are released under CC BY 4.0 and the code under the MIT license.

detail.abstract: Search frictions normally raise the bar for sorting: both random and directed search require complementarities strictly stronger than the supermodularity that suffices in Becker's (1973) frictionless model. We introduce private information into this setting: firms post wages without observing worker productivity, while better workers have better outside options, creating a market for lemons (Akerlof 1970). We show that this information friction pushes sorting the other way: attracting high-productivity workers without attracting low-productivity ones requires a higher wage paired with a lower job-finding probability, so vacancies fill faster. This strict ranking of vacancy-filling rates sorts the market positively whenever output is complementary in worker and firm quality. Becker's condition therefore suffices once more, and private information makes positive sorting easier to sustain than complete information does.

detail.abstract: Final constitutional courts decide questions of meaning in ways that political institutions can seldom correct, and the standard defences of that power place legitimacy in interpretive method or in respect for precedent. This article examines whether either defence can bear the weight placed on it. Through a doctrinal, jurisprudential and comparative-institutional analysis of the United States, Germany and the European Union, the United Kingdom and Canada, and Brazil, it asks how the burden of justification borne by a constitutional court should be structured so that judicial power remains democratically accountable. The literature review shows that scholarship on interpretive method and scholarship on precedent have largely developed separately, and that the traditional rationale for weaker constitutional stare decisis, the difficulty of democratic correction, has not been systematically examined for its implications for the act of overruling. The article argues that this rationale is symmetrical: because a constitutional overruling is as difficult to correct as the original decision, the rationale supports re-examination of precedent but not low-cost reversal. It proposes that the burden of justification be calibrated to the reversibility profile of the judicial act, meaning the degree to which the act forecloses response by actors other than the court. A five-element standard of justification, assembled from existing practice including Brazilian procedural law, follows from the analysis as a consequence and not as a free-standing framework. The article addresses the democratic, realist and originalist objections, states conditions under which the thesis would be weakened, and acknowledges its doctrinal rather than empirical character. Its contribution is a doctrinal and normative argument about where the burden of judicial justification should lie. detail.abstract: National constitutional courts increasingly resist transnational authority by invoking "constitutional identity", yet the concept is applied to quite different disputes and with quite different consequences. This article asks under what conditions an identity-based reservation against transnational authority is justified, and what separates justified from abusive invocation. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis, it examines authorities from Germany, Italy, France, the Czech Republic, Poland, India, Colombia, Brazil, Argentina and Russia, together with the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union, the European Court of Human Rights and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights. It distinguishes three sites of identity review: against supranational integration, against constitutional amendment, and against international adjudication. The literature, which tends to treat each site separately and to define identity by its content, leaves unresolved how courts and external observers can evaluate a reservation without adopting a substantive theory of any one nation's character. The article argues that the legitimacy of a reservation turns on its function rather than its content: a reservation is justified to the extent that it protects the conditions of constitutional self-government (rights-bearing, democratically accountable and independently adjudicated public power), and loses justification when it shields the incumbent exercise of power from the very checks those conditions require. The same test applies, symmetrically, to claims of transnational primacy. The contribution is doctrinal and normative, not empirical; it is qualified by its dependence on published authorities and by the indeterminacy of the test. detail.abstract: Copy-trading marketplaces publish complete position histories, recorded server side, for every signal they sell. This paper takes eight such books from the largest marketplace, 29,143 closed positions from 2020-11-13 to 2026-07-31, and reads them with three instruments that need nothing beyond the ledger and an independent price feed: a structural integrity screen, an exposure-concentration multiplier, and the exitinvariant violation statistic that certifies entry information per unit traded. A 28-symbol reference layer, sixteen native hourly histories plus twelve triangular synthetics, matches 99.4% of in-window FX positions, 18,450 trades against a pilot coverage of 3.5%. The population is not what a buyer of track records imagines: three of eight books are grid machines that escalate size after losses with up to 48 simultaneous same-symbol positions, four more stack heavily, one is clean, and one trades instruments no majorcurrency feed can price. Per-trade statistics understate true exposure by up to 7.7 times. One book turns a losing entry stream,-4.22 pips per unit at-4.9 standard errors, into a dollar violation of +0.80 per trade at t = +20.2 purely by sizing into winners, a twentysigma artefact of evaluation currency. Three stacked books and the single clean book read genuine per-unit entry information at three to thirteen standard errors; the pooled readable population carries +2.25 pips at t = 2.6.

detail.abstract: Chienge District, on the north-eastern shore of Lake Mweru in Luapula Province, combines a productive artisanal fishery, a hinterland in Zambia’s largest cassava-growing province, and a border with the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). Yet it lies in a province where 77.3 percent of people were poor in 2022 and 45 percent of children under five were stunted in 2024, against a national rate of 32 percent. This paper is a desk-based synthesis of national statistics, road-agency and contractor records, and peer-reviewed fisheries and political-ecology research. It asks why the district’s assets have not generated broad-based income, and which interventions are both effective and achievable within Zambia’s institutional and fiscal constraints. Five findings emerge. First, physical isolation is being addressed by a 95-kilometre, K1.96 billion road upgrade that was 11 percent complete in August 2026 and is contractually due around December 2028. Second, the Lake Mweru–Luapula fishery is more resilient, and more rainfall-driven, than the “tragedy of the commons” narrative implies, but its village comanagement committees are under-funded, vulnerable to elite capture and weakly enforced. Third, value addition is constrained by unreliable power, an absent cold chain and limited cassava processing. Fourth, cassava yields are depressed by disease, for which a locally tested remedy exists, while claims of land exhaustion remain untested. Fifth, no post-2022 districtlevel estimates of poverty, electricity access or child nutrition are published, so targeting is necessarily imprecise. The paper proposes sixteen measures, each screened for legal mandate, cost, delivery capacity and time to first result, and sorted into those to start now, those conditional on financing or demand, and options to prepare. Early priorities are reform and financing of village fisheries management committees beginning with the 2026/27 closed season, landing-site catch monitoring, clean cassava planting material, a demand-anchored solar-and-ice pilot, nutrition programming and a district baseline. The paper also states what it does not recommend at present, including large processing plants, aquaculture, mineral surveys and large irrigation schemes. A monitoring framework with realistic targets and an impact-evaluation design is provided. Figures should be read as indicative because Chienge-specific data are sparse.

detail.abstract: This study examined the relationship between population dynamics and unemployment trends in Nigeria from 1986 to 2024. The study investigated the effects of population growth, fertility rate, dependency ratio, educational attainment and urbanization on unemployment, while Gross Domestic Product (GDP) was included as a control variable. Annual time-series data were obtained primarily from the World Development Indicators and supplemented with National Bureau of Statistics and Central Bank of Nigeria sources. An ex-post facto research design was adopted and the Autoregressive Distributed Lag (ARDL) bounds-testing framework was employed to estimate short-run and long-run relationships. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller test showed a mixture of I(0) and I(1) variables, with none integrated at I(2). The bounds test produced an Fstatistic of 6.242683, exceeding the 5% upper critical bound of 3.28, indicating a long-run relationship among the variables. The error-correction coefficient was-0.689225 (p=0.0000), indicating that approximately 68.9% of short-run disequilibrium is corrected annually. Long-run estimates show that dependency ratio and urbanization are positive and statistically significant determinants of unemployment, while GDP is negative and significant. Population growth, fertility rate and education have statistically insignificant long-run coefficients, although education has the expected negative sign. Granger causality results indicate unidirectional causality from urbanization to unemployment. Diagnostic tests indicate normally distributed residuals, no serial correlation and no heteroskedasticity.

title: Understanding inflation: insights from the term structure of inflation risks

detail.abstract: This paper investigates the information content of the term structure of inflation risks and its usefulness for understanding inflation dynamics. Using prices of traded zero-coupon inflation caps and floors, we develop a robust non-parametric methodology, combined with a Student’s t-copula, to estimate spot and forward risk-neutral densities at short-, medium-, and long-term horizons, i.e., long-horizon risks are identified from liquid instruments alone, at daily frequency, without forward-starting contracts. Focusing on the euro area over 2009-2026, we show that the term structure of inflation risks provides valuable information about the persistence of inflation shocks and the degree to which changes in the inflation outlook become embedded at longer horizons. We also show that there is marked heterogeneity in the macroeconomic and financial conditions associated to inflation risks across horizons: short- and medium-term risks are mainly associated with current inflation, confidence indicators, commodity prices, and near-term macroeconomic risks, whereas long-term risks are more strongly related to monetary and financial conditions. These findings highlight the importance of analysing the entire term structure of inflation risks rather than relying on a single maturity.

detail.title: Disruption in the Classroom: Experimental Evidence from Ecuador
detail.abstract: We study how poorly-behaved children affect learning and other outcomes of their peers using data from a unique experiment in Ecuador. Within each school, students were randomly assigned to classrooms in every grade for seven consecutive grades, between kindergarten and 6th grade. Children with persistent behavioral problems lower the math and language achievement of their classmates. The more poorly-behaved children there are in a classroom, the larger is their negative impact on the achievement of their classmates. These negative impacts are larger for younger children, and they persist for at least two years after exposure to a poorly-behaved peer. There are no dynamic complementarities in the impact of poorly-behaved peers: impacts are similar for children who were and were not previously exposed to poorly-behaved peers (and for high and low ability children). We find indirect evidence that children with persistent behavioral difficulties are passed around schools.

title: The Automated State: A Realist View
affiliations: Stanford Law School

detail.title: The Automated State: A Realist View

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract:
Government use of artificial intelligence ("AI") to make, implement, and enforce law is fueling anxieties among a growing cast of critics. Some are accelerations of concerns raised by other technology adoptions: error, bias, gaming, and the oversight challenges that come with reliance on procurement. Others are more AI-specific: the power of machine learning and big data to draw privacy-violating inferences, or AI's "black box" opacity and inability to engage in democratic reason-giving. The reforms AI's critics demand in response range from the sharp and specific (e.g., outright prohibitions and full-blown, Food and Drug Administration-like licensure) to the gauzy and unproven (e.g., calls to "democratize AI" via participatory design or impact assessments).

This Essay sketches an alternative, "realist" view in three parts. First, policymakers are unlikely to enact the bespoke new regulation of the sort critics are demanding because of AI's twin capacity to cause and cure error, bias, and inequity. For every horror story there will be a success story-a way new tech makes government's work more efficient, accurate, rule-of-law-respecting, and equitable. Second, public law has always been radically limited in reach relative to critics' demands. Indeed, even progressive commentators have long warned that the problem with government may not be too little transparency, but too much, and new procedural burdens, however well-meaning, can stultify a government that already lacks vigor. A final insight follows: the urgent task ahead may be both more pedestrian and more ambitious than AI's critics suggest. Indeed, if algorithmic accountability will be litigated rather than legislated, then efforts should focus more than they have on legal adaptation-that is, the tailoring of existing legal frameworks, particularly ordinary administrative law, to the government's new algorithmic toolkit. Wise adaptation, not the blue-sky regulatory overhauls that occupy much of the scholarly literature, should be the order of the day. This Essay makes a start down that road.

detail.abstract: Leveraging the unique setting of unilateral euroisation, this paper examines the spillover effects of euro area monetary policy on Montenegro and Kosovo. Through the lens of a structural VAR model with block exogeneity, it shows that euro area monetary policy shocks can significantly influence output and inflation in these economies, albeit with a delayed response, while contributing only modestly to their overall business cycle fluctuations.

detail.abstract:
This paper examines how the economic activities in the Brazilian Monthly Trade Survey (PMC) have contributed to the aggregate retail sales volume index throughout its history. Our primary contribution is the quantification of activity-level trend, seasonal, and irregular components of the PMC restricted index. This is achieved by combining Restricted Least Squares weight recovery with independent Prophet-based decompositions for each of the eight retail activities, which are then aggregated through a bottom-up approach. The recovered weights for the 2022 base year match IBGE's officially published figures, and estimated weights prior to 2022 are consistent with the documented revisions, replicating the aggregate index almost exactly.

Supermarkets emerge as the main driver of the retail index's trend, anchoring the aggregate's long-run evolution given their structural weight and relative stability. Pharmaceuticals, meanwhile, stand out as the only activity with uninterrupted trend growth over the sample. Seasonal behavior is most intense in Books & Stationery and Apparel, though their contributions to the aggregate end up diluted by smaller weights in both cases. During the 2020–2021 period, the initial negative shock is concentrated in Apparel and Others, April 2020's collapse is driven predominantly by external disturbances, and the recovery that followed reflected autoregressive propagation instead.

A forecasting exercise over the last 24 observations confirms reasonable out-of-sample predictions, and bottom-up aggregation of activity-level forecasts improves accuracy relative to the direct aggregate-level Prophet benchmark. Despite not being optimized for forecasting performance when compared to other approaches such as X-13-ARIMA, our results are consistent with the paper's primary objective of stable and interpretable structural decomposition.

Note: This is a Working Paper, comments and suggestions are welcome.

detail.abstract:
Background: Randomized trials of adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after endovascular reperfusion of large vessel occlusion stroke reported inconsistent average treatment effects. This study aimed to investigate individualized treatment effects (ITEs) of adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis after endovascular reperfusion using machine learning approaches.

Methods: This was a secondary analysis of the POST-UK and POST-TNK trials. Both trials enrolled patients with anterior-circulation large vessel occlusion who achieved near-complete to complete endovascular reperfusion. A machine learning model was developed in POST-UK (n=532) to estimate ITEs of adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis and was subsequently validated in POST-TNK (n=539). The primary outcome was freedom from disability, defined as a 90-day modified Rankin Scale (mRS) score of 0–1.

Findings: In the POST-TNK validation cohort, predicted ITEs ranged from -25.0% to +32.8% for adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis versus control, with positive values favoring adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis. Patients predicted to benefit from adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis had a multivariable profile characterized by more frequent cardioembolic, greater neurological deficit, relatively preserved ASPECTS, lower systolic blood pressure, and higher baseline glucose levels. Predicted ITE strata modified the effect of adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis on freedom from disability at 90 days significantly (P for interaction = 0.01). In exploratory analysis based on the model, assignment to the treatment strategy predicted to be best for each patient was estimated to increase the absolute rate of freedom from disability by 5.7%.

Interpretation: Adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis individualized using machine learning analyses of randomized trials may improve freedom from disability after successful endovascular reperfusion. A prospective trial evaluating individualized use of adjunctive intra-arterial thrombolysis is needed.

detail.abstract:
Background: Childhood otologic disease is a leading, preventable cause of hearing loss in sub-Saharan Africa, yet Nigeria lacks direct-examination data comparing rural and urban children within one state to guide school-based screening policy. We determined the prevalence, pattern, and correlates of otologic disorders among primary school children in rural and urban Edo State, Nigeria.

Methods: This community-based, comparative cross-sectional study used multi-stage random sampling to recruit children aged 5 to 16 years from Egor (urban) and Etsako East (rural) Local Government Areas of Edo State. Each child underwent bilateral otoscopy, tympanometry, and pure-tone audiometry; sociodemographic data were collected by interviewer-administered questionnaire. Associations were assessed with Pearson's chi-square or Fisher's exact test and multivariable logistic regression.

Findings: We examined 1356 children (759 urban, 597 rural; 88·6% aged 6 to 12 years). At least one otologic disorder was present in 887 (65·4%, 95% CI 62·8 to 67·9): 503 of 759 (66·3%) urban and 384 of 597 (64·3%) rural. Impacted cerumen was the most common (605, 44·6%), followed by otitis media with effusion (102, 7·5%), otitis externa (53, 3·9%), chronic suppurative otitis media (39, 2·9%), and bilateral hearing loss (38, 2·8%). After adjustment, urban schooling (AOR 2·35, 95% CI 1·67 to 3·30), Edo ethnicity (AOR 1·44, 1·05 to 1·96), extended-family structure (AOR 1·65, 1·12 to 2·44), higher birth order (AOR 1·95, 1·26 to 3·02), lower primary class (AOR 1·68, 1·15 to 2·47), and low paternal education (AOR 1·66, 1·19 to 2·32) were independently associated with disease.

Interpretation: Two in three primary school children in this Nigerian state had a clinically detectable, largely preventable or treatable ear disorder, with distinct risk profiles by setting. These findings support embedding structured ear and hearing screening within Nigeria's National School Health Policy, tailored to urban crowding and rural service-access gaps rather than a uniform rural-deficit assumption.

title: Fintech in the Global South: Rewriting Regulatory Convergence in Financial Regulation
affiliations: Singapore Management University - Singapore Management University Yong Pung How School of Law

detail.title: Fintech in the Global South: Rewriting Regulatory Convergence in Financial Regulation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author has no conflicts of interest to declare.

affiliations.org_name: Singapore Management University - Singapore Management University Yong Pung How School of Law

detail.abstract: Financial regulation is usually narrated through the institutional history of the Global North, with the financial centers of New York, London, Frankfurt, and, more recently, Singapore and Hong Kong serving as the standard comparative baseline for financial technologies. The rest of the world, particularly the Global South, is presumed to converge toward those models. This article argues that, in a series of crucial domains in fintech regulation, the premise is backwards. Drawing on the concept of legal heterodoxy, it contends that the Global South has become a major site of regulatory invention in fintech precisely because it has had to solve foundational problems of access, interoperability, inclusion, market concentration, and consumer vulnerability at speed and scale. Jurisdictions such as India, Brazil, Thailand, the Philippines, Malaysia, Nigeria, Colombia, China, and Indonesia have not merely adapted Northern templates. They have crafted distinctive legal and institutional forms, including public instantpayment infrastructures, bespoke digital-bank licensing regimes, ecosystem-wide anti-fraud mechanisms, and activity-based oversight of non-bank and platform-based financial intermediation. The article develops this argument in four steps. First, it shows why legal heterodoxy is a useful framework for understanding fintech regulation outside the traditional centers of finance. Second, it examines four domains of Global South regulatory innovation: instant digital payments, digital banking, liability and risk allocation in payment fraud, and the regulation of embedded finance and non-bank intermediaries. Third, it identifies a growing pattern of South-South convergence around shared design principles such as interoperability, central-bank stewardship, proportionate licensing, and function-based supervision. Finally, it argues that fintech regulation exhibits a reverse convergence, understood as a shift in the direction of comparative attention. The Global South is no longer simply a recipient of international financial-regulatory models in the fintech space but an increasingly important, and contested, source of them.

detail.abstract: We study a generalization of the BLP random coefficient demand model in which consumers have heterogeneous tastes for unobserved product quality. When the random coefficient on unobserved quality is almost surely positive and enters through a quality index, the share map is globally invertible and the model is identified; without the sign restriction, invertibility can fail. The key result is that the Jacobian of the share map is everywhere a nonsingular M-matrix. The standard BLP fixed-point iteration need not converge in this setting, and a sufficient global step-size bound can become arbitrarily small. We establish global convergence of alternative nonlinear iterations and develop a damped Newton method that is globally convergent and, under a mild local smoothness condition, locally quadratic. Monte Carlo experiments with endogenous Bertrand-Nash prices confirm the computational results and show that imposing homogeneous tastes for unobserved quality can substantially distort preference estimates and substitution patterns, with product-level cross-price elasticities differing by about 20 percent in our baseline design.

detail.abstract: We provide new evidence on the international spillover effects of US monetary policy through global commercial real estate (CRE) markets. Using a global VAR-X model that exploits both city- and country-level data, we account for spatial dependencies arising from cross-border investor ownership of CRE. A US quantitative easing shock leads to a persistent rise in CRE prices, both within and outside the US, and an expansion of credit, but mostly in the US. To interpret these findings, we develop an open economy New Keynesian model with CRE markets, which highlights the role of increased domestic demand for foreign CRE as a key transmission channel. Moreover, the model reveals that spillover effects can spill back to the US via trade linkages, amplifying the initial effects of US monetary policy.

detail.abstract: Economic growth depends on combining existing inputs into new inventions. However, these combinations are not always physically feasible. One important example is dark silicon, where power and cooling limits prevent all the transistors on a chip from operating at once. I develop a growth model motivated by these limitations and establish conditions for a unique balanced growth path where electronic miniaturization and power efficiency grow at the same rate. When power-efficiency research becomes harder, both total research employment and productivity growth fall on the new balanced growth path. With gradual adjustment of research employment, I construct a local equilibrium transition in which more researchers temporarily coexist with slower productivity growth. This Eroom's law result holds for small shocks in a two-dimensional design space with sufficiently similar industry constraints.

detail.abstract:
Student Stress and the Need for Positive Coping

Students in Illinois face a growing crisis of stress and mental health. Nearly 45% of children have experienced at least one adverse childhood experience (ACE), and 29% of high school students report poor mental health in the past 30 days. Yet schools have historically lacked evidence-based practices and programs to help students build positive coping skills, leaving children to navigate stress without the tools they need.

In response, Illinois enacted S.B. 2872 (Public Act 103-0764; effective January 1, 2025). This bill allows school districts to set aside at least 20 minutes per week for student relaxation activities, including meditation, breathing, stretching, mindful movement, and yoga. Illinois is among the first states to codify this range of well-being practices. The diversity of activities listed creates both a dynamic opportunity to address student stress and a responsibility to effectively implement activities that are appropriate to students’ needs. This policy spotlight examines the evidence supporting Illinois’s new law and offers actionable recommendations for turning policy into practice.

What the Evidence Shows: Mindfulness Works

Decades of research—including multiple studies by the authors (Dariotis et al., 2016, 2023, 2025, 2026)—consistently demonstrate that mindfulness-based interventions (MBIs) produce measurable benefits for students from preschool through high school:

▪ Reduced behavioral and emotional difficulties: lower rumination, fewer intrusive thoughts, and decreased emotional arousal.
▪ Improved emotional regulation and impulse control: greater ability to recognize emotions, empathize, and take others’ perspectives.
▪ Stronger academic performance: consistent positive effects on academic outcomes according to meta-analytic evidence (Verhaeghen, 2023).
▪ Increased physiological benefits: improved nervous system regulation that buffers students against stress reactivity, even as young as preschool-aged.
▪ Additional peer multiplier effects: transfer of practices by students to siblings, peers, and family members, which extended impact beyond the classroom at no additional cost.

Recent evidence further underscores these findings. A school-based mindfulness program demonstrated significant benefits for marginalized high school students in urban communities (Dariotis et al., 2023). Another study (Gould et al., 2012) among elementary school aged children found mindfulness helped reduce negative coping strategies that are beyond one’s immediate control (referred to as involuntary engagement – like rumination, intrusive thoughts, emotional arousal) with varying levels of effectiveness among youth reported depressive symptoms

detail.abstract: Amenity-based models have outperformed job-based models in explaining long-run regional growth in the United States. Those models, however, treat a location's climate as belonging to that location alone. This paper argues that the climate a household actually consumes is the best annual profile it can assemble from places within easy reach. Because households dislike joint extremes of heat and cold, regions in which two complementary climates lie close together offer a valuable option: residents can spend part of the year, or respond to particular weather events, in the other place. The option is available through second homes, rentals and short trips, and its value falls steeply with travel time. Complementary pairs require topographic relief or a coastline, so flat regions lack them whether hot or cold. The framework yields predictions for second-home ownership holding wealth constant, for the timing and flexibility of second-home use, for vacation travel to cold places as population shifts toward warm ones, and for long-run regional growth. It identifies two routes by which households avoid joint extremes-uniform climates and complementary pairs-and notes that California, strong on both, has nonetheless experienced net domestic out-migration, an anomaly addressed in a companion paper.

detail.abstract: Long-run U.S. population movements have been driven more by natural amenities than by jobs, and California, rich in both uniform and complementary climates, should be a persistent net gainer of domestic migrants. It has instead lost residents to other states every year since about 1990. This paper argues that its amenities are unchanged and that the location rents they generate have been captured politically. Capture through a land tax would be borne by landowners and would move no one. Capture through mobile tax bases-above all a steeply progressive income tax-and through restrictions on housing supply does move people, and moves particular people. Where the revenue also finances redistribution, high earners pay far more than the value of the services they receive, which pushes them out on a second count; the income tax also raises the pre-tax wages firms must pay, so jobs leave with households. Proposition 13 shifts capture onto mobile tax bases and locks long-tenured owners in place, so observed out-migration understates the underlying pressure. Internal Revenue Service data show that in 2022-23 California's out-migrants outnumbered its in-migrants by 40 percent overall but by 64 percent among households with incomes of $200,000 or more, a pattern reversed in low-tax states. A simple cross-state comparison, which cannot hold production advantages constant, shows no relation between tax burdens and natural amenities, suggesting that competition among amenity-rich states limits capture; California, which taxes well beyond what its neighbors charge, loses residents disproportionately to them. Border comparisons and data on homeowners' length of residence are consistent with the argument.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how New York City's congestion surcharge affects passenger tipping behavior in yellow and boro taxis (green taxis). Using trip-level data from NYC Open Data and a difference-indifferences framework, I find that tip percentages increase by approximately 2.6 percentage points for yellow taxis and 2.7-6.8 percentage points for boro taxis after the policy. Tipping responses vary across trip characteristics and the fare distribution, with stronger effects for slow trips and greater heterogeneity across fare levels for boro taxis. Overall, the results suggest that passengers adjust tipping behavior in response to salient, policy-related price changes, and the responses vary with trip characteristics and fare composition. The findings highlight tipping as an important margin through which transportation pricing policies affect consumer behavior.

detail.abstract: Population allows a country to become consequential to the international order long before its people become rich. A follower with four times the leader's population reaches aggregate parity at one quarter of the leader's income, with three leader-sized economies of catch-up still ahead. Population also lowers the income at which a home market and an engineering pool can sustain a broad set of frontier sectors. This paper connects that divergence to the political supply of diffusion. The leader earns rents from the network it sustains: other countries gain more inside it than they could obtain outside. Ordinary commerce within that network diffuses knowledge, and a populous follower can build a credible alternative on the strength of its home market. Other countries' outside options then improve and the leader's rents fall, even if no one leaves and trade keeps growing. In a contested relationship the leader can therefore restrict knowledge-bearing access while cooperation is still creating value. At equal aggregate size, a more populous follower sets in motion a larger prospective erosion from the same diffusion opportunity. I call the feedback endogenous diffusion congestion: success reduces the supply of the diffusion that produced it. Restrictions are most valuable on the inputs that complete an independent capability and lose force once substitutes exist. Historical comparisons separate population, compatibility, and control. India provides a prospective test of whether cooperation can accommodate broad autonomous capabilities in a country that remains far from income parity.

detail.abstract: Mexico taxes flavored drinks with added sweeteners through a specific excise (IEPS) charged per liter. On November 7, 2025 a decree published in the Diario Oficial de la Federación raised the quota on sugar-sweetened drinks from 1.6451 to 3.0818 pesos per liter and, for the first time, extended the tax to drinks sweetened only with non-caloric 'edulcorantes' at 1.5000 pesos per liter, effective January 1, 2026. This paper measures how much of that tax reached retail shelf prices, using 1,448,631 product-level price observations in PROFECO's open 'Quién es Quién en los Precios' database for January of 2024 to July of 2026. A difference-indifferences design with brand-by-package-size and month fixed effects, using never-taxed bottled water as the control, estimates a pass-through of 1.01 for added-sugar drinks (coefficient +1.445 pesos per liter, s.e. 0.092) and 0.38 for edulcorante drinks. Placebo reform dates produce effects of a fifth to a tenth of this size, so the result is not a mechanical reflection of a general price trend. Near-full pass-through means consumers were the ones to absorb the 2026 increase as opposed to bottlers or retailers, and the new edulcorante quota narrowed the shelf-price gap between regular and diet versions of the same brand.

detail.abstract: Can history say which model portfolio suits a given risk aversion? We compare five fixed-weight portfolios differing only in equity share (20 to 100 percent), with the portfolios, costs, metrics and a grid of 17 risk-aversion levels recorded in an author-maintained hash registry before any result was computed, and run the same contract on Korean won data from 2001 (308 months) and U.S. dollar data from 1990 (434 months). First, at no risk-aversion level could the certainty-equivalent leader be told apart from the runner-up (0 of 68 comparisons); with intervals several points wide, this reflects low power, not evidence that the portfolios are equal. Second, a trend overlay cut the drawdowns of the equity-heavy rungs at up to 327% annual turnover, yet its certainty equivalent was indistinguishable from that of fixed weights in all 170 comparisons. Third, return, volatility and maximum drawdown rose with the equity share, and 60/40 fell between the 50% and 70% rungs, marginally above all five at four of 34 grid points (no registered interval). Because drawdowns were strictly ordered as point values, we read the tables by drawdown; that reading rule was written into the dollar edition only, after the won results were seen, and is a selection criterion, not a tested result or advice. title: Long-Run Trends in the Age of Labor Market Entry

affiliations.org_name: University of Erlangen-Nuremberg-Friedrich Alexander Universität Erlangen Nürnberg

detail.abstract: Demographic aging causes substantial worker shortages. So far, policy debates neglect the aspect of age at labor market entry. We study the age at which young individuals first enter the labor market and how it has developed over the last four decades. Based on long-running administrative data, we describe birth cohorts from 1960 through 2000, and separately consider different types of employment entry. We investigate the entry age distribution and heterogeneities across demographic groups. We find that conditional on employment, the median age of first holding a stable full-time employment increased by almost 4 years between the birth cohorts 1960 and 1995. Our decomposition analysis yields that more than one quarter of this increase is explained by higher educational attainment and the rising share of non-German workers, which appear to be the main mechanisms behind the delay in labor market entry. Additionally accounting for changed occupations, industry composition, and relative entry-level earnings explains about 40 percent of the observed delay in labor market entry. The role of different mechanisms varies across the types of employment entry.

title: AI-driven Technological Progress, Finite Change and Wages
affiliations: Department of Economics, Jadavpur University, University of Texas at San Antonio - College of Business - Department of Economics, Hanyang University Erica Campus, Birla Institute of Technology (BIT), Mesra and Indian Institute of Foreign Trade

detail.title: AI-driven Technological Progress, Finite Change and Wages

affiliations.org_name: University of Texas at San Antonio - Department of Economics
CESifo (Center for Economic Studies and Ifo Institute)

detail.abstract: When technological progress uniformly raises the productivity of all factors of production within a competitive industry, it typically increases the real returns to those factors — including the wage rate in that industry. This mechanism plausibly reflects the nature of AI-driven technological progress. In standard general-equilibrium setting, the rest of the economy adjusts endogenously to such a shock, preserving the factor-return gains of the progressing sector. We depart from this framework by introducing Finite Change, which permits a non-progressing industry to contract fully and exit equilibrium, thereby mimicking the forced redundancy of sectors displaced by AI-enabled technologies. While “small” technological shocks preserve the wage gains of the advancing sector in general equilibrium, we show that sufficiently “large” shocks — i.e., Finite Change — can overturn this outcome, leaving workers in the initially advancing sector worse off. Notably, this reversal can arise even when the initial technological improvement occurs exclusively in the labor-intensive industry, a result that cannot be obtained in models restricted to marginal (infinitesimal) changes.

title: Gang Crackdowns
