detail.abstract: What are the consequences of restoring state authority in territories governed by criminal organizations? Combining household surveys and administrative records with detailed maps of former gang-controlled areas, we study how El Salvador’s 2022 State of Exception, which ended two decades of gang territorial control, reshaped Salvadoran society. We find that the removal of gang control integrated previously segmented labor markets, improving mobility, employment outcomes, household income, and financial inclusion. Areas with greater pre-2022 gang exposure also experienced larger increases in business formation and property investment. However, the legacy of criminal governance persists through residence-based discrimination: employers remain less willing to hire otherwise identical applicants from former gang-controlled neighborhoods. Finally, although overall support for the crackdowns remains high, individuals who witnessed police abuse report substantially greater distrust of the police and the national government, suggesting that abuses of state authority may undermine the political sustainability of tough-on-crime policies.

title: A Cyclical Long Memory Model for US Unemployment

detail.abstract: This paper examines the cyclical structure of the monthly US unemployment rate using an approach that differs from the stationary I(0) and unit root cycle ones. In particular, the model specification allows for the spectrum to explode at a frequency away from zero. This long memory component enables us to approximate the length of the cycle such that shocks can have transitory but persistent effects. The empirical results show the adequacy of the proposed framework to capture the observed behaviour of the monthly US unemployment rate.

title: Dynamic Risk Externalities, Institutional Inertia, and the Limits of Viability
affiliations: Karlsruhe Institute of Technology and University of Greifswald - Department of Economics

detail.title: Dynamic Risk Externalities, Institutional Inertia, and the Limits of Viability

affiliations.org_name: University of Greifswald - Department of Economics

detail.abstract: Rapid technological change can generate risks that extend beyond the actors creating them, while institutional capacity to contain these risks adjusts only gradually. Strategic rivalry can reinforce this mismatch by sustaining incentives for technological acceleration even as risk increases. The interaction of endogenous risk creation with institutional inertia can therefore transform a quantitative imbalance between risk creation and governance-capacity formation into a qualitative viability problem: beyond a critical boundary, a low-risk equilibrium ceases to exist. We develop a differential game in which countries choose technological acceleration and governance mobilization. These flows accumulate into technological capability, a common risk stock, and effective governance capacity. Technological capability has productive and strategic value, whereas aggregate acceleration generates risk that is only partially internalized. Rising risk strengthens incentives for containment but can simultaneously increase the strategic value of relative technological capability. Governance mobilization responds to risk but becomes effective only as it is gradually converted into governance capacity. Relative to a multilateral cooperative benchmark, the non-cooperative equilibrium features excessive technological acceleration and insufficient governance mobilization. We map these equilibrium responses into a two-dimensional risk--governance system, which yields an endogenous viability frontier. "Low-risk'' denotes an equilibrium in which accumulated governance capacity is sufficient to balance endogenous risk creation; it does not imply intrinsically low or socially optimal risk. Institutional delay can therefore shift the policy problem from correcting an externality toward preserving a dynamically sustainable balance between risk creation and governance capacity. We apply the framework to current AI policy configurations and AI-enabled synthetic biology. Rapid and increasingly distributed technological capability raises informational, monitoring, and coordination requirements for effective safeguards and can narrow the margin within which risk creation remains dynamically containable.

title: Impact of the economic recession on the business structure: opportunities, threats and risk of insolvency

detail.abstract: Economic recessions represent one of the most significant challenges to business continuity because they simultaneously affect liquidity, access to credit, demand levels, and organizational stability. This paper examines the impact of recessionary environments on corporate structures from a business insolvency perspective, analyzing both the threats and opportunities that emerge during periods of economic contraction. It argues that recessions rarely constitute the primary cause of insolvency; rather, they tend to expose and accelerate pre-existing vulnerabilities related to excessive leverage, weak risk management, inadequate financial planning, and obsolete business models. Through the analysis of recent corporate experiences, the study shows how recessionary shocks influence strategic decision-making, organizational restructuring, resource allocation, and business adaptation. The paper concludes that resilience, financial discipline, and the capacity to reassess business models are critical determinants of whether firms succumb to insolvency or transform economic adversity into a catalyst for renewal and long-term sustainability.

detail.abstract: We study the transmission between non-core and core inflation with the clustered network connectedness framework of Buchwalter et al. (2026a), a new method that, unlike the generalized variance decompositions of the traditional Diebold-Yilmaz approach, separates contagion between groups of variables from co-movement within them. We apply it to the components of Peru's consumer price index, extend it to the frequency domain and add a cluster of external controls to measure transmission net of common external shocks. With noncore prices ordered first, non-core inflation is a net transmitter to core inflation throughout the sample, whereas generalized decompositions classify it as a net receiver for most of the period before 2021. Contagion from non-core to core inflation rises sharply after 2021, while transmission in the opposite direction remains stable, and the increase occurs mainly at long-run frequencies, consistent with a gradual pass-through. Controlling for external shocks leaves contagion before 2021 almost unchanged but reduces its subsequent increase by more than half. These results are robust to the lag order, the window length, the definition of frequency bands and the set of controls.

title: Strategic Infrastructure, Ordinary Rules: Energy, Water, and Sovereignty Risks in Chile's Data Center Regulation

detail.abstract: Chile has emerged as Latin America's leading candidate for becoming a data center regional hub, yet its regulatory framework treats hyperscale digital infrastructure as ordinary industrial real estate, assessing it for land-use compatibility and environmental impact without addressing systemic energy, water, and sovereignty risks. This paper argues that Chile's current governance model underestimates the structural dimensions of data center development, thereby increasing financing uncertainty. Drawing on the comparative experience of Virginia's incentive-driven model (which produced a structural energy cost crisis) and Singapore's sustainability-conditioned framework (which demonstrates that regulatory ambition and investment attractiveness are not mutually exclusive), the paper proposes four targeted reforms: a tariff classification and cost attribution mechanism; a tiered grid priority regime; climatic zone-differentiated water efficiency standards; and a narrowly scoped foreign investment screening mechanism. Together, these proposals establish a regulatory architecture that protects investors, ratepayers, communities, and the Chilean State, before the sector's political weight forecloses the opportunity for binding reform.

detail.abstract:
Does handing a neural encoder a quantity it could compute from its other inputs change the representation it learns? We test this in a pre-registered comparison of input views of the limit order book, B6: NEST adds to the book's ladder 8 scalars that are exact, bit-identical functions of it and SUBST does not, so before the input transform the views differ in duplication, not information. Over 3 architectures, 3 objectives and 3 seeds on 5 spot pairs, each cell's NEST-to-SUBST similarity is compared with the similarity between seeds of one view. Per asset, B6-H1 (different representations) needs the shortfall below that seed ceiling to be permutation-significant in at least 6 of 9 cells, to average at least 0.1 in CKA and to be confirmed by mKNN; B6-H0 (the same) needs it to be neither significant nor that large; each needs 4 of 5 assets. B6-H1 is NOT SUPPORTED (0 of 5) and B6-H0 is NOT SUPPORTED (0 of 5): the significance clause holds on 5 of 5 assets and the margin clause on 0, and a shortfall larger than permutation noise and smaller than the size the design declared meaningful supports neither. As the design's reading stated before any figure existed, the significance clause asks little more than a positive shortfall, so the margin carries the evidence; on it alone, a reading that is not criterial, B6-H0 holds on 5 of 5 assets. Every figure is generated from the experiment's artifacts and checked by an independent verifier.

detail.abstract: A currency board ties the Hong Kong dollar to the US dollar, so the rate that governs a shopping trip into the mainland is the dollar's rate against the renminbi. Research on hard pegs has concentrated on aggregate outcomes such as output and inflation, and the cross-border shopping literature has measured price gaps that a local government sets through a tax or a devaluation; in neither setting is that price fixed by a peg. This paper asks how much of the movement in retail sales value the HKD/CNY rate accounts for, which measures a channel through which imported monetary policy reaches the household sector without passing through interest rates. Using monthly retail sales from 2004 to 2026, excluding 2020--2022, when the boundary was closed, we estimate the reduced form over the two boundary-open periods. Our estimate of the elasticity of retail sales value with respect to the cross rate lies between -1.3 and -1.9; it recurs at similar magnitude in the two periods, which span two decades of very different mainland conditions. It survives holding mainland visitor arrivals constant, which rules out the reading that the rate merely proxies for visitor demand. The contraction is concentrated in goods that can be carried across the boundary, and within the 2023--2026 reopening a one percent appreciation raises northbound departures by about six percent. For a small open economy with a land border, then, the exchange-rate regime shapes retail activity through the household's trip.

title: A Uniform Bounded-Real Criterion for Quadratic-Gaussian Term-Structure Existence
affiliations: Independent Researcher, USA and Kspectra Research Inc.

detail.abstract: Quadratic-Gaussian term-structure models price bonds by quadratic-exponential moments, which can be infinite: once the loading Riccati equation escapes, longer bonds have no finite price, and no fit to the liquid range shows it. Nor does admissibility at a low factor count imply it at a higher one. For the frozen quadratic sector of a damped oscillator lattice with rank-one integrated source, one maturity integration makes the stationary-source problem exactly bounded-real. At each truncation N the threshold η * N is sharp for the stationary flow; the running flow is global below an explicit η * * N and escapes above η * N. Both decrease to positive limits given by one supremum of an explicit gain: η < η * * ∞ certifies every truncation, uniformly in dimension and maturity, while η > η * ∞ makes every sufficiently fine one fail. Below η * * ∞ , loadings converge at the maturity-uniform upper rate O(N-1/2), and pinched blocks, oscillator cells and, under scalar stability, conditional prices on bounded retained states at O(N-1). The autonomous long-maturity convexity density is finite at the boundary but has divergent sensitivity. The normalised fixed-and dense-lattice thresholds have noncommuting linewidth asymptotics, and an explicit matched profile quantifies the crossover when the linewidth-to-spacing ratio is held fixed. For the coupled system we give an exact finite-dimensional conjugate-point criterion and a dimension-free safe region; inside that region the coupled integrated loadings converge to a unique global infiniteresolution flow at the finite-window rate O(N-1/2). The sharp coupled boundary remains open.

title: Valuing the Protective Benefits of Natural Resources through Recreation Demand under a Safety Constraint
affiliations: Tohoku Gakuin University

detail.abstract: This paper develops a static model of visitation demand for a natural resource that provides both recreational and protective functions. Visitors face a safety constraint under which the subjective probability of severe harm must not exceed an individual tolerance limit. The protective function reduces expected monetary loss conditional on a disaster and lowers the conditional probability of severe harm, thereby relaxing the safety constraint. When the safety constraint is strictly binding, a reduction in travel cost does not increase visitation, whereas an improvement in the protective function does. The marginal protective benefit decomposes into the effect of reducing expected loss and the welfare gain from relaxing the safety constraint. Under quasi-linear utility, a fixed tolerance limit, and weak complementarity, the total protective benefit equals the area between the constrained visitation demand curves before and after the improvement. Numerical examples further show that omitting the safety constraint does not systematically produce a smaller protective benefit: relative to the constrained model, the benefit can be either larger or smaller. These results highlight the importance of accounting for safety-related limits on visitation when valuing the protective functions of natural resources.

title: The Right Wing of the SABR Smile with an Absorbing Boundary: Resolution of Conjectures of Henry-Labordère
affiliations: Independent Researcher, USA and Kspectra Research Inc.

detail.title: The Right Wing of the SABR Smile with an Absorbing Boundary: Resolution of Conjectures of Henry-Labordère

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None.

detail.abstract: We determine the extreme fixed-maturity right wing of the SABR model with elasticity parameter strictly between zero and one and absorption at zero. The leading logarithmic decay rate of the terminal right tail exhibits a phase transition at zero correlation. For nonnegative correlation, it coincides with the rate predicted by the unrestricted hyperbolic geometry. For negative correlation, paths generating large terminal values must also avoid the absorbing boundary, and this survival requirement creates an additional leading-order boundary-crossing cost. A model-free transfer principle converts the tail asymptotics into the corresponding Black–Scholes implied-volatility wing. Consequently, Henry-Labordère’s conjectured right-wing limit is valid for nonnegative correlation but fails for every negative correlation. We also show that boundedness of the scalar potential at the unrestricted saddle point is insufficient to justify the associated Gaussian wing estimate. The correct model-specific geometric quantity is the intrinsic Riemannian distance within the survival domain, equivalently the state space of the killed subprocess. The proof combines a stopped Lamperti–CEV transform, conditional Brownian time change, Gaussian moving-boundary estimates, finite-dimensional convexity, and matching change-of-measure lower bounds. No general Dirichlet heat-kernel estimate is assumed.

title: Emerging Applications of Consonant-Vowel (CV) Mnemonics
affiliations: Center for Creative Foresight

detail.abstract: Digital systems rely on compact codes to identify people, places, transactions, objects, and machine states, yet such codes are often difficult for humans to remember, communicate, compare, or verify. The Consonant-Vowel (CV) Mnemonic method addresses this problem by mapping every two-digit value from 00 to 99 to a pronounceable consonant-vowel pair. Later work extended the approach to geographic coordinates through Open Geo-Mnemonic (OGEM) coding and to AI-generated visual mnemonics. This article reviews these developments alongside research on memory, chunking, phonological encoding, visual mnemonics, authentication, and geocoding. It surveys applications ranging from security codes, device pairing, transaction references, logistics, and geographic locations to CV grids, AI-agent identifiers, digital fingerprints, sensory profiles, and facial-likeness proxies. It argues that CV is best understood as a human-readable layer over existing machine systems, with generative AI supporting optimization, semantic elaboration, imagery, personalization, and recognition while preserving the underlying canonical code.

detail.abstract: This article reviews how economists use differences in patent examiners’ tendencies to study the effect of patent rights. When examiner assignment is effectively random and other identifying assumptions hold, these differences create “accidental experiments” that help isolate the consequences of patent protection. The literature provides evidence on startup growth and financing, inventor mobility, litigation, and the importance of patent scope and examination delays. However, the credibility of the estimates depends on a careful understanding of administrative practices. Examiner specialization and changes in application routing can undermine the assumption of quasi-random assignment.

detail.abstract: Day-ahead and real-time electricity prices differ by the DART spread. Hours with the largest absolute spreads carry much of the price risk in two-settlement markets. Automated trading and risk systems can use models to identify those node-hours for position sizing and downstream directional logic. A fixed score cutoff determines how often this high-spike signal activates. If the score distribution shifts, the same cutoff can flag far more or far fewer hours than intended while ranking metrics (AUC, AUPRC) show nothing wrong. We audit this cutoff drift across 33 nodes and four U.S. operators from 2023 to 2026. Cutoff placement alone has a large effect: with the model, features, and deployment window fixed, using in-sample rather than held-out scores changes the median realized-to-target alert ratio from 1.7 to 0.20, about eightfold. A sealed 2026 test rejects the development-period prediction that absolute-price features would be least stable. A matched audit then separates a robust result from a pipeline-specific one. With periodic recalibration, plain lagged DART spreads keep their realized alert rate near its target across both periods and both models, while absolute levels fail in 2024-25 under both models. In 2026, the full DART-relative family is less stable than absolute levels only in the rolling-origin boosted-tree pipeline; this ordering does not occur under rolling-origin logistic regression or in the frozen-origin boosted-tree system. Cutoff stability therefore belongs to the whole deployment pipeline, not to the features alone. Simple input-drift measures do not reliably identify the failing family, so deployed systems should monitor the realized alert rate directly.

title: Rotating Leadership and Coalitional Stability
affiliations: Uppsala University - Department of Economics, Friedrich-Schiller-Universität Jena, UniDistance Suisse and Uppsala University

detail.title: Rotating Leadership and Coalitional Stability
detail.abstract: Rotating leadership is prevalent in international relations. Examples include the presidencies of the EU Council, the G7, and the African Union. Why would self-interested actors take turns rather than, for instance, have a permanent leader? We study this question in a repeated three-player coordination game of conflicting interests, where agents want to coordinate on a common action (leadership), but disagree on what is the best action to coordinate on (who should lead at any point in time). Standard subgame perfection provides no answer to the research question since it allows for many leadership arrangements, including a permanent leader, or the exclusion of one agent from leadership, or fully rotating leadership. We show, however, that they differ in robustness to coalitional deviations. Asymmetric arrangements give disadvantaged players persistent incentives to form a breakaway coalition against the incumbent. By evenly distributing leadership opportunities, full rotation emerges as the most stable self-enforcing institution. Results from a preregistered laboratory experiment support the relevance of this mechanism also to interpersonal relations: rotations predominate when interests are highly heterogeneous, while permanent leadership arises mainly when interests are relatively aligned. Refuting predictions from inequality aversion, rotations remain predominant even when one player receives an additional choice-independent lump-sum income, while strategies aimed at reducing this payoff gap remain rare. This suggests that the risk of coalitional breakdown is an important driver of why also individuals – not just nations – share decision making evenly.

title: Optimal Paternalistic Regulation of Markets
affiliations: CREST - Ecole polytechnique and Ecole Polytechnique, Palaiseau - Department of Economics

detail.title: Optimal Paternalistic Regulation of Markets

affiliations.org_name: University College London - Department of Economics
Ecole Polytechnique, Palaiseau - Department of Economics

detail.abstract: Many markets are regulated for paternalistic reasons. We develop a mechanism-design framework to derive the optimal policy mix between price regulation and quantity controls. A budget-constrained planner allocates trade between privately informed buyers and sellers while disagreeing with their valuations. When the planner’s valuations preserve the ranking of agents, price instruments (e.g., sin taxes) are optimal. When the planner instead believes that a high willingness to trade indicates a bias, optimal regulation can restrict quantities or even prohibit transactions. De-biasing interventions offer two benefits beyond economic regulation: improving selection into markets and, for virtuous goods, raising the volume of trade.

title: PF-Mamba-UNet: An Anatomical-Prior-Guided Medical Image Segmentation Network Based on Mamba and Spatial-Channel Collaborative Attention Fusion

detail.title: PF-Mamba-UNet: An Anatomical-Prior-Guided Medical Image Segmentation Network Based on Mamba and Spatial-Channel Collaborative Attention Fusion
detail.abstract: Medical image segmentation plays a pivotal role in clinical diagnosis assistance, lesion detection, and computer-aided medicine. However, factors such as complex organ boundary morphologies, multi-scale structural variations, and low contrast continue to pose challenges for accurate segmentation. To address this, this paper proposes an efficient segmentation network based on the fusion of anatomical prior and features—Anatomical-prior-guided Fusion Mamba-UNet (PF-Mamba-UNet). Firstly, the CR-VSS module is designed. Within the VSS module, a convolutional refinement branch is constructed to enhance local detail modeling. An integrated CSS2D module enables multi-directional scanning along horizontal, vertical, diagonal, and anti-diagonal paths, boosting the model's multi-directional perception and feature capture capabilities for complex geometries. Secondly, the Coordinated Spatial-Channel Fusion Attention (CSCFA) module is designed and embedded in the skip-connection layers of the encoder and decoder. Through a spatial-first mechanism, it synergistically enhances spatial and channel features, thereby highlighting critical anatomical regions while suppressing redundant background noise. Finally, an anatomical prior regularization is constructed to balance boundary smoothing and regional consistency. The former ensures continuity and smoothness of segmentation edges, while the latter guarantees structural consistency within regions. Collectively, they ensure the anatomical plausibility and structural continuity of segmentation results. Medical image segmentation results demonstrate that PF-Mamba-UNet exhibits significant performance advantages over mainstream models including U-Net, SwinUNet, Mamba-UNet, Mamba-Sea, KM-Unet and CSWin-Unet.

detail.abstract: Researcher degrees of freedom, enabled by publication incentives, can produce a literature in which results are selected for statistical significance. We develop an approach to stress testing an economic literature using Foghorn, a declarative econometric framework that makes empirical choices explicit, concise, and modifiable. After independently replicating approximately 79% of the M&A studies meeting our sample criteria, we vary the construction of the dependent variable, control variable definitions, and sample selection using alternative design choices found within the literature. Across more than 4,500 tests using alternative dependent variable constructions, baseline t-statistics for the key explanatory variable exceed alternatives in 80% of cases, and 37% of alternatives lose significance at 10%. This baseline advantage is significantly smaller for controls, consistent with specification selection associated with publication incentives. As LLMs lower the cost of searching for significant results, our approach enables the scrutiny of specification dependence.

detail.abstract: The European Union has placed learning for sustainability at the intersection of the European Education Area and the European Green Deal. Yet education remains primarily a responsibility of the Member States, while teaching and curriculum decisions are further mediated by national institutions, schools, and professional communities. This article examines how the European Union coordinates education for the green transition under these conditions. It presents a qualitative document analysis of the strategic framework for European cooperation in education and training, the 2022 Council Recommendation on learning for the green transition and sustainable development, GreenComp, and the Education for Climate Coalition. The analysis distinguishes three complementary modes of coordination: political coordination through common objectives and reporting expectations; cognitive coordination through a shared competence vocabulary; and networked coordination through voluntary communities of practice. The findings show that these instruments create a layered soft-governance architecture rather than a unified curriculum or implementation regime. This architecture can support policy learning and cross-border exchange, but its non-binding character does not by itself guarantee pedagogical autonomy. Autonomy also depends on how competence frameworks, monitoring practices, funding incentives, and participation formats are translated into national and local contexts. The article argues that legitimate European coordination should preserve contestability, contextual adaptation, and professional judgement while strengthening feedback between European frameworks and educational practice. It concludes by identifying conditions under which European sustainability education can combine strategic direction with educational pluralism.

detail.abstract: We examine how creditors price a landmark expansion in financially distressed firms' opportunities to engage in corporate political activity. Using the U.S. Supreme Court's decision in Citizens United and daily five-year CDS spreads, we find a non-monotonic response: CDS spreads increase most for firms with moderate pre-decision lobbying, rather than for those with the highest or lowest lobbying. These firms combine a demonstrated propensity to participate in politics with meaningful scope to expand that participation. CEO political donations and firms' subsequent lobbying behavior reinforce this interpretation. We also exploit the ruling's additional effect in states that previously restricted corporate independent political expenditures. The CDS response is particularly strong when CEOs' prior donations reveal engagement with the headquartersstate political environment. Finally, the response is amplified among firms with high pre-decision net debt and attenuated when outstanding loans contain debt covenants, consistent with debt-related concerns. More broadly, our evidence shows that campaign-finance rules can have financial-market consequences even before any subsequent political expenditure or policy outcome is observed.

detail.abstract:
Background Reproductive health outcomes across sub-Saharan Africa. In Ethiopia, these milestones have largely been studied separately. We assessed social and geographic inequalities in reproductive timing across four milestones within a common analytical framework.

Methods: We analyzed cross-sectional data from a Performance Monitoring for Action (PMA) survey conducted in Ethiopia in 2023, including 8,943 women aged 15–49 years. Survey-weighted Kaplan–Meier methods estimated age at each milestone. Survey-weighted multivariable Cox models assessed associations with residence, household wealth, education, region, and religion. Proportional hazards assumptions were assessed using Schoenfeld residuals; educational associations were modelled across attained-age periods because of non-proportionality.

Findings: Rural women experienced first sexual intercourse (median 18·0 vs 20·0 years), first union (18·1 vs 21·0), and first live birth (20·1 vs 23·0) earlier than urban women, but initiated contraceptive use later (27·0 vs 23·0). After adjustment, rural residence remained associated only with earlier first union (adjusted HR 1·17, 95% CI 1·00–1·36). Educational level showed consistent associations across all four outcomes. Wealth differences were largely attenuated except for contraceptive use, while regional differences persisted. Education by attained age period interactions were significant for all outcomes, with educational differences in first sexual intercourse, first union, and first live birth greatest at younger ages, and attenuating with age.

Interpretation: Reproductive timing inequalities in Ethiopia extend beyond an urban–rural divide. Educational attainment and region were important dimensions, while contraceptive initiation showed a distinct socioeconomic pattern.

title: Coarse by Design: Risk Communication and the Oregon Wildfire Map

detail.abstract: Governments communicate risk through coarse categories. I show that when private behavior generates spillovers, a coarse but truthful risk disclosure can strictly dominate detailed disclosure, even for fully rational individuals. Coarseness is a second-best policy instrument: expanding the high-risk category draws additional individuals into private action that protects others. I apply this framework to Oregon's 2022 Wildfire Risk Map, which assigned each of the state's two million parcels to one of five risk categories and drew intense backlash from owners disputing its accuracy. I first show that Oregon's free model predicts held-out fires about as well as the leading proprietary alternatives. The map's coarse categories embed a trade-off between false alarms and misses, which I recover from the boundary of the high-risk category: over the two decades of fires the state could observe, catching one additional fire costs roughly twenty-five flagged parcels that do not burn. Given external estimates of adaptation costs and effectiveness, this permissive boundary is consistent with a planner who internalizes spillovers. Moving this boundary traces the set of maps that planners with different preferences over false alarms and misses would have drawn.

detail.abstract:
This Special Issue is prompted by a confluence of developments in higher education: increasing access to postsecondary schooling overall and concurrent increasing socioeconomic inequality. After World War II, American colleges and universities began to “massify,” expanding their enrollments by opening their doors to people who previously would have found them closed. First, these institutions admitted veterans, then people of color and women (Altbach and Reisberg 2018, p. 63; Gumport et al. 1997, p. 2; Labaree 2017, pp. 106–7). The U.S. was not an outlier, and in the ensuing decades, nations around the globe saw unprecedented increases in the number of students pursuing a college degree (Trow 2001, p. 245). This growth in enrollments seemed likely to expand opportunity and potentially to reduce socioeconomic disparities as an increasing share of the population benefited from the financial opportunities associated with higher education. Yet that did not happen. Instead, dramatic increases in access to higher education have coexisted with rising levels of inequality. In fact, the level of wealth inequality among Americans today rivals that seen on the eve of World War II, shortly before the process of massification began (Piketty 2014, p. 76, fig. 1.1). 

These trends, seemingly in tension, raise intriguing questions. Why and how did massification, reflecting a democratic impulse toward wider accessibility of higher education, occur alongside stratification in higher education, contributing to wealth and income inequality? How did colleges and universities successfully massify, radically expanding overall enrollment and the diffusion of higher education, even as inequality increased? Why did massification fail to disrupt inequality? Did the stratification among colleges and universities, in fact, perpetuate inequality? How did the declining role of public, direct funding of higher education—especially in the U.S.—contribute to these phenomena? 

To understand these dynamics fully, we must consider the multiple ways in which wealth-based disparities shape higher education, affecting what kind of student enrolls at what kind of institution with what sort of outcome. This Special Issue begins with articles that address access to higher education. Much of the debate over wealth-based disparities in the United States focuses on access, particularly the role of persistent increases in college tuition, rising student debt burdens, and their effects on less affluent students. The cost of getting a degree can seem daunting, prompting low-income students to forego college, postpone their studies, attend college part-time, or even drop out (Sanchez et al. 2024, p. 4). Low-income students who do pursue higher education may attend college burdened by the constant worry of finding themselves homeless or hungry on campus (Broton and Goldrick-Rab 2018, p. 122; Hallett et al. 2019, pp. 8–9). These students may also feel less able to access elite social networks, in which affluence is taken as a given, that confer competitive advantages in employment after completion (Jack 2019, p. 9; Rosales et al. 2024, p. 50). Moreover, wealth-based differences can shape the lives of college students long after graduation. Students dealing with substantial educational debt may be reluctant to take on new financial obligations and so may put off potentially costly life changes, including marriage, parenthood, and homeownership (Jabbari et al. 2023, p. 2; Martinez et al. 2024, p. 9). 

The challenging questions prompted by the twin phenomena of greater access and increasing inequality do not arise only in the United States. Although there is much to be learned from the American system of higher education, this Special Issue puts those lessons in an international context. Nations around the globe have sought to massify their institutions of higher education (Trow 1999, pp. 315–19). National governments have deployed different strategies to expand enrollment capacity, and these efforts have proceeded at different paces across these different contexts (Pan and Luo 2008, p. 76). Yet, these nations—like the United States—have seen connections between socioeconomic status and educational opportunity (Buckner and Abdelaziz 2023, p. 547; Ilie et al. 2021, p. 1254; Krafft and Alawode 2018, p. 31; Torche 2011, pp. 798–99).

detail.abstract: Between 1880 and 1912, concern about the movement and sexual exploitation of women and girls became an increasingly visible issue in English public life. What later came to be described as anti-trafficking activism was closely connected to older campaigns against prostitution, the sexual exploitation of children, and state regulation of prostitution. Yet the campaign was not simply about protecting women. It was also shaped by ideas about masculinity, national responsibility, morality, class and the changing image of England as an imperial nation. This article examines the relationship between masculinity and anti-trafficking activism in England between 1880 and 1912. It argues that the protection of women became one way through which men and male-dominated institutions attempted to demonstrate moral authority, social responsibility and national strength. The period witnessed important developments in organised anti-trafficking activity. The campaigns associated with Josephine Butler and the repeal of the Contagious Diseases Acts had already challenged the sexual double standard, while Alfred Stace Dyer's 1880 publication on English girls abroad helped bring the language of "white slavery" into a more prominent anti-trafficking campaign.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relationship between retail gasoline prices and gasoline consumption in the United States using 192 monthly observations from January 2010 through December 2025. Monthly U.S. Energy Information Administration data on retail gasoline prices and product supplied of finished motor gasoline are combined with real disposable personal income data from the Federal Reserve Economic Data database. A log-log multiple regression model is estimated with monthly controls to account for seasonality. The estimated gasoline price coefficient is negative but statistically insignificant, indicating that the full-sample analysis does not provide strong evidence of a stable relationship between gasoline prices and consumption. Seasonal effects are considerably stronger, with gasoline consumption generally higher during the summer months. Validation using autocorrelation-robust inference and sensitivity analysis around the COVID-19 period further indicates that the estimated price relationship is specification-sensitive. The findings suggest that businesses operating in the gasoline market should avoid relying on a single national price elasticity for decision-making and should incorporate seasonality, local market conditions, costs, and broader economic factors into demand forecasting and pricing decisions.

title: Deportation Judges: Executive Capture of the Immigration Courts
affiliations: University of Idaho College of Law

detail.title: Deportation Judges: Executive Capture of the Immigration Courts

detail.abstract:
Recent changes to immigration courts have transformed them from tribunals organized around evidentiary adjudication to immigration enforcement collaborators. This shift can be seen in the adoption of summary removal policies, an increased number of in absentia orders of removal, and decreases in the share of completed cases that include an evidentiary hearing. These changes have begun to collapse the distinction between expedited removal proceedings, which historically applied to noncitizens apprehended near the border soon after entrance, and immigration court cases for noncitizens in the interior, which traditionally involved greater due process protections, including evidentiary hearings.

The Trump administration has achieved this change by radically reworking court procedures and substantive immigration law through Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA) and Attorney General (AG) precedential decisions and EOIR policy memoranda. The changes both streamline proceedings and make it harder for noncitizens to win. In addition, the administration has purged the corps of IJs and hired replacements consisting largely of former military lawyers, former lawyers for Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and other former prosecutors. Tellingly, in its recruitment materials, the administration has referred to the position as “Deportation Judge.” These Deportation Judges have presided over a sharp decline in grant rates for asylum and other relief and a sharp rise in deportation orders.

It is not normal in a democratic system for a president to tell judges how to decide cases, even when it comes to courts housed in executive agencies.  Rather, decisional independence is critical for the rule of law, separation of powers, and the protection of individual rights. On the other hand, court manipulation is normal in authoritarian systems, where courts serve other purposes, such as enforcing social control, legitimatizing the system, and delegating controversial reforms to judicial institutions. This essay analyzes recent changes to immigration courts in light of the scholarship concerning the purposes and impact of courts in authoritarian systems, concluding that the Trump administration’s capture of the immigration courts reflects a slippage into authoritarianism. Relatedly, it considers how to approach immigration court reform from a transitional justice framework. The essay presents a proposal for a path forward that establishes judicial independence, copes with the large backlog of immigration court cases generated by heightened immigration enforcement, and reckons with an era of immigration injustice.

title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business and MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Lab (CSAIL)

detail.title: How exposed is work to robotics? Occupational, industry, and geographic measures

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no personal or financial relationships with other people or organizations that could have inappropriately influenced this work.

detail.abstract:
Exposure indices that map technical capabilities onto occupational abilities have become a standard tool for anticipating how AI may reshape work, but existing measures either cover software AI or proxy robotics through patents and installation data that reflect the industrial robots of past decades. We construct the first abilities-based exposure measures for robotics and physical AI, and the first to span occupations, industries, and geographies. Following the framework of Felten et al. (2018, 2021), we build a robotics capability taxonomy of 16 capabilities in eight domains from 78 academic, industry, and standards sources, use a large language model to score the relatedness of each capability to the 52 O{*}NET work abilities, and aggregate to Robotics Occupational Exposure (ROE) for 774 occupations, Robotics Industry Exposure (RIE) for 250 NAICS industries, and county-level Robotics Geographic Exposure (RGE).
We find that robotics exposure concentrates in physically intensive work such as construction, farming, transportation, and production, and in industries such as logging, mining, trucking, and warehousing. Unlike generative-AI exposure, ROE is higher in occupations with lower wages, lower education requirements, and less creative-ability content. Physical collaboration and assistance, terrain-based locomotion, grasping and handling, and task and functional reasoning move the exposure ranking most, yet no single capability carries the index. Because the measures capture technical relatedness rather than readiness, cost, or adoption, they should be read as an upper bound on where physical automation could affect work.

title: Full calibration, fast simulation, and exotic options pricing under the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck driven stochastic volatility model
affiliations: University of Pavia - Department of Economics and Management and Politecnico di Milano- Dipartimento di Matematica

detail.title: Full calibration, fast simulation, and exotic options pricing under the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck driven stochastic volatility model

detail.abstract: We propose efficient methodologies for calibrating and simulating the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck-driven stochastic volatility (OUSV) model and for pricing frequently monitored exotic options. First, we provide a new representation of the characteristic function of log-returns which (i) avoids discontinuities caused by branch switchings of complex functions; and (ii) it is easy to differentiate with respect to the model parameters. Based on this, we propose a fast, full calibration algorithm that exploits the analytical gradient to speed up computations. Second, we develop a low-bias simulation scheme that is fast and accurate. It is theoretically motivated and works well for both large and small time steps, making it ideal for pricing path-dependent options. Extensive numerical studies demonstrate the superiority of the proposed simulation methodologies over existing benchmarks. Third, we derive the characteristic function of integrated logarithmic returns and propose an efficient method for pricing geometric Asian options that are monitored continuously or discretely, based on the Fourier-cosine method. Finally, we address the issue of efficiently pricing exotic options using Monte Carlo simulation. We combine the low-bias simulation scheme with: (i) the new geometric Asian option pricing procedure, creating a Monte Carlo control variate approach for pricing arithmetic Asian options under the OUSV model; and (ii) the new expression for the characteristic function of log-returns, efficiently pricing barrier options using a conditional Monte Carlo method. The calibration and simulation algorithms presented in this paper satisfy the speed and accuracy requirements for practical trading.

title: More Distribution Without More Agents: The RANKFULL New Keynesian Model
affiliations: Maverick Institute

detail.abstract: Representative-agent New Keynesian (RANK) models achieve tractability by compressing household behavior into a single representative household, but that aggregation can discard economically relevant information about who receives changes in income. When households differ in their marginal expenditure responses, two income-incidence patterns can generate the same aggregate income change yet produce different aggregate-demand effects. Heterogeneous-agent models can capture these differences, but at the cost of substantially greater household-sector complexity. I develop RANKFULL, a distributionally augmented RANK framework that restores only the distributional information required for a specified macroeconomic response. For the baseline expenditure application, I show that aggregate income is sufficient if and only if the relevant marginal expenditure responses are identical across household groups. When they differ, only one additional scalar distributional statistic is required at first order, regardless of the number of empirical household groups used to construct it. Embedding this statistic in the standard New Keynesian aggregate-demand block allows income incidence to affect output, inflation, and monetary-policy responses while preserving the representative household, Phillips curve, and policy rule of the parent RANK model. The framework yields an empirical sufficiency test and a model-selection principle: retain RANK when aggregate information is sufficient, use RANKFULL when the missing distributional information is low dimensional, and move to TANK or HANK when heterogeneous household decisions or the endogenous distribution are themselves central to the mechanism.

detail.abstract: Chest radiography interpretation remains constrained by a global radiologist shortage. Most automated systems address detection or report generation in isolation, and fewer still have been evaluated on openly available datasets that include paired radiologist text for simultaneous quality measurement.,This paper presents RadVision AI — a complete, deployable pipeline that integrates a DenseNet-121 multi-label classifier pre-trained on 1.3 million radiographs, Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (GradCAM) for spatial lesion indication, and Claude Sonnet 4.5 for structured report generation. The system is implemented as a full-stack web application comprising a Python/Flask backend, React 18 frontend with three simultaneous imaging views (annotated, high-contrast enhanced, pseudo-colour segmented), client-side PDF report generation, and a physician validation module with deployment-readiness scoring.,Evaluation against 200 frontal radiographs from the Indiana University Chest X-Ray collection (IU X-Ray) — which provides both MeSH disease labels and free-text radiologist reports — yields a mean AUC of 0.677 across eight evaluatable conditions, ranging from 0.310 for emphysema to 0.982 for hernia. An ablation study with matched 200-image samples confirms that GradCAM does not alter disease probability estimates, producing identical AUC across both configurations while yielding a marginal improvement in report text similarity (BLEU-1: +0.002, ROUGE-L: +0.002). 6 of 14 target conditions had 0 positive examples in evaluation sample, indicating the IU X-Ray outpatient population rather than model failure — a significant outcome determined transparently.,The entire codebase, evaluation pipeline, and pre-trained weights are publicly released to support reproducible medical AI research in resource-confined institutions.

detail.abstract:
Background: The human hip is an evolutionarily derived load-bearing system functioning across increasingly prolonged lifespans and changing environments. Across Asian regions and North Africa and the Middle East (NAME), where stages of demographic transition differ markedly, we examined temporal and life-course changes in the burden and composition of GBD-identifiable hip-specific conditions.

Methods: We analysed hip osteoarthritis, hip fracture, and hip dislocation from 1990 to 2023 across six Asian regions. We assessed incidence and years lived with disability (YLDs), age-sex patterns, relative composition and dominance, osteoarthritis-fracture balance, and decomposed changes in absolute YLDs into population growth, population ageing, and epidemiological change. All derived compositional and decomposition indicators were calculated from point estimates and interpreted descriptively.

Findings: Absolute YLDs increased for all three conditions in every region. Hip fracture age-standardised YLD rates declined in all six regions despite increasing absolute YLDs. The proportion of combined YLDs occurring at age ≥ 55 years  increased everywhere, reaching 78.2% in East Asia and 91.0% in high-income Asia Pacific in 2023. Osteoarthritis increased as a share of YLDs in five regions, but fracture remained the leading contributor across nearly all age-year strata; osteoarthritis dominance was confined to the oldest ages in Central Asia. In people younger than 20 years, dislocation accounted for 55.9-71.1% of incident cases, whereas fracture accounted for 81.6-87.4% of YLDs. Population ageing was the largest positive contributor to combined YLD growth in East Asia and high-income Asia Pacific, whereas population growth predominated in South Asia and NAME; epidemiological change partly offset demographic increases.

Interpretation: Hip-related disability is expanding, shifting towards later life, and being reweighted, but these processes are not epidemiologically equivalent. Surveillance should distinguish absolute burden, age-standardised trends, incident events, and accumulated disability. Prevention and care should prioritise preservation of mobility across the life course, with service capacity scaled to regional demographic trajectories.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how a government should strategically select an experimental design to assess a new crop variety's market potential and disclose this information to guide smallholder farmers' cropping and production decisions. We develop a game-theoretic model where farmers first choose between a traditional crop with stable market performance and a new variety with uncertain demand and then engage in Cournot quantity competition. The government commits ex ante to an experimental design that maps market states into public signals. Applying the Bayesian persuasion framework, we characterize the welfare-maximizing information policy and show that full disclosure is optimal only when demand volatility is sufficiently high; otherwise, partial disclosure is optimal. The results follow from a trade-off between a disclosure effect that improves quantity decisions through reducing uncertainty and a diversification effect that mitigates market concentration by sustaining crop heterogeneity. This trade-off generates a counter-intuitive comparative static. Within the partial-disclosure region, higher prior expected demand can shift the optimal policy from optimistic to pessimistic disclosure, moderating adoption incentives to prevent excessive concentration and protect margins. Extensions capturing developing-economy features, including asymmetric information access and alternative dissemination channels, confirm the robustness of the mechanisms and policy implications.

detail.abstract: Research on remote electronic voting has concentrated on the security of a single election, treating voting credentials as static objects of indefinite validity. A system operated as national infrastructure across a decade cannot sustain that assumption: bearer credentials are lost, cryptographic standards age, and electorates turn over. The accumulated effect erodes security and equity together, and permanent, uncounted disenfranchisement gathers among the holders a recovery channel failed to reach. No existing framework measures this irrecoverable loss under the anonymity constraint that forbids retaining any individual participation history, nor turns such a measurement into an accountable decision to reissue credentials. This paper develops the Adaptive Renewal Policy (ARP)-the policy of renewing a credential series, not of rotating keys-to fill that gap. Its core is a differential anchored indicator that estimates irrecoverable loss from aggregates alone, comparing the non-recovery-bound population against a recovery-bound control group. The control group absorbs the background attrition a raw count would misread. Three invariance corrections-anchoring on first use, window-eligibility, and lagged classification-make the indicator robust to voluntary abstention and remove a registration campaign from the evaluation at which it occurs, leaving at most a bounded level shift afterwards. Around the indicator the paper builds: (i) an algorithm enforcing privacy constraints through hardwaremediated aggregation; (ii) a threat model for the attacks a public threshold invites, including hostile recovery registration and a governance attack on the recovery lineage; (iii) a theoretical analysis showing that increments (not levels) carry the evidence, that horizon-dependence of the optimal threshold is resolved by a committed threshold paired with bounded council discretion, and that the cost of forcing an unnecessary renewal diverges as adversarial targeting degrades toward random; and (iv) a Monte Carlo validation of the indicator and its decision rules against an explicit hypothesis set. A comparison with five alternative lifecycle policies is deliberately even-handed, characterising precisely the conditions under which adaptive renewal is the right choice: expensive re-issuance, a binding anonymity requirement, and a credible governance body. Stated for any bearer-credential voting system that partitions voters into a recovery-protected and an exposed group-the precondition the differential indicator requires-rather than for one architecture, the framework offers a first systematic account of credential-lifecycle governance for anonymous remote electronic voting.

title: Does Matching Contribution Incentivize Informal Workers to Participate in Retirement Saving Plans? A Randomized Evaluation Interacted with a Natural Experiment

detail.title: Does Matching Contribution Incentivize Informal Workers to Participate in Retirement Saving Plans? A Randomized Evaluation Interacted with a Natural Experiment
detail.abstract:
We conducted a large field experiment in Peru on informal workers and studied whether offering them a matching contribution raise participation and contributions in their Individual Retirement Accounts. We had three groups: a control group receiving no match, and two treatments groups receiving 50 and 100 percent match, respectively. Additionally, due to the time span, we can also analyze the difference responses between pre and during Covid-19. The results were as follows. First, the match incentive increases participation. Workers in the 50 and 100 percent match groups show participation rates of 5.2 and 6.5 p.p. higher than workers in the control group, respectively. The participation effect is also present pre Covid-19 and disappears during it. Second, the 100 percent match incentive was the only effective in increasing savings among all individuals (1.4 p.p.), pre (2.3 p.p.) and during Covid-19 (0.97 p.p.). This effect still presents in LATE specification with higher p.p. Third, 100% match was again the only effective to make contribute more than once, in the full sample (1.2 p.p.), and pre Covid-19 (2.7 p.p.), including LATE specification (full sample – 5.6 p.p.; pre Covid-19 – 8.2p.p.). Fourth the 50 percent match is not effective in raising contribution in any specification.

detail.abstract: This article reviews Daphne Barak-Erez’s Biblical Judgments: New Legal Readings in the Hebrew Bible,evaluating the book’s contribution from a legal and theoretical perspective and situating it within the broader discourse on reading biblical texts as a foundation for modern legal thought. While acknowledging the project’s scope and its achievement in making biblical legal dilemmas accessible to contemporary readers, the review highlights its weaknesses: fragmenting the texts, relying on an intuitive method of interpretation, and risking anachronism. As an alternative, it proposes a living originalist approach that emphasizes the layered nature of biblical texts and their development from multiple sources, editorial strata, and diverse voices. Using the story of Naboth’s vineyard as a test case, the analysis demonstrates that the final product is a multi-layered legal text that includes diverse perspectives on justice, kingship, prophecy, and law. These viewpoints resist simple categorization and instead create a sense of arguments, messages, and explanations that move back and forth across the theological, political, and legal importance of the story. The complexity and sophistication of this narrative have enabled later generations to treat it as authoritative and to adapt it to their own needs.

detail.abstract: This paper presents seven design lessons for practitioner-built AI decision support systems, that is, systems conceived and assembled by domain experts without a dedicated software engineering team, using agentic AI development tools. The lessons are derived by conceptual synthesis from a reference design documented in a companion research series (a two-stage multi-criteria decision framework, a serverless client-side architecture, a multi-agent build method, and a governance framework) and from the surrounding literature on multi-criteria decision making, sensitivity analysis, serverless computing, large language model (LLM) agents, and AI governance. The reference design addresses the prioritization of entities in a capacity-constrained logistics distribution network. It is illustrated here only with a synthetic dataset of 1,500 generated records; no operational data, deployment, or user observations are reported. The lessons concern: composite scoring with a single dominant criterion; tier-based pre-sorting as a hard governance boundary; client-side computation for interactive analytics; multi-agent specialization as a quality-governance mechanism; serverless-first infrastructure selection; a conversational interface as a primary access path; and documentation as concurrent governance. For each lesson we state the design decision, the rationale and literature support, and what the synthetic demonstration does and does not show. For example, the tier boundary yields zero cross-tier violations in 1,000 Monte Carlo weight draws by construction, whereas the stability of a top-ranked anchor entity varies across synthetic datasets (mean 0.899 over 20 replications). A portfolio map (Table 2) relates each lesson to its source in the companion papers. The lessons are conceptual propositions that have not been validated in the field, and we outline the field studies that would test them.

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether the right to die can be recognised as a fundamental right by implication under the Constitution of Kenya, 2010. It analyses the right to life under Article 26 alongside individual autonomy, human dignity, health, and constitutional interpretation. Particular attention is given to the High Court's decision in Kenya National Commission on Human Rights & 2 others v Attorney General & 3 others [2025] KEHC 6 (KLR), which declared the criminalisation of attempted suicide unconstitutional. The paper argues that, although Kenyan law does not expressly recognise a right to die, the constitutional framework and emerging jurisprudence may support a limited negative dimension of the right to life. It therefore recommends further judicial and legislative consideration of whether such a right may exist in constitutionally defined circumstances.

detail.title: Capital Structure, Cost of Capital, and Value Creation: An Empirical Study

detail.abstract:
In the highly leveraged world of auto manufacturing, taking on debt is usually just part of the game. But Bosch Limited, a heavyweight tier-1 automotive supplier listed on both the NSE and BSE, plays by a very different set of rules. This paper delivers the financial playbook of Bosch, exploring how the company structures its capital, prices it, and ultimately translates those choices into real shareholder value. By digging through five years of audited standalone financials (FY 2021-22 to FY 2025-26), we set to see if Bosch's strictly zero-debt approach actually holds up when pitted against traditional corporate finance theories. To put some hard numbers behind this strategy, we used the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and the Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) to figure out the company's true hurdle rate. The math simply confirms what anyone glancing at their balance sheet already suspects: Bosch is completely unlevered. With a debt-to-equity ratio of exactly 0.00x, equity carries the entire 100% weight. Plugging in a 7.10% risk-free rate, an adjusted beta of 0.85, and a 6.00% equity risk premium, both the cost of equity and the WACC settle right at 12.20%. It's a straightforward mathematical reality-when you have zero debt, your WACC is just your cost of equity. 

But does this conservative approach leave money on the table? To find out, we benchmarked Bosch against two industry peers: Schaeffler India and Samvardhana Motherson International. While these competitors use debt to lower their nominal WACC via interest tax shields, Bosch clearly prioritizes long-term solvency and operational flexibility. And the strategy is paying off. Bosch is generating a Return on Capital Employed (ROCE) of 21.54%. Since that easily clears their 12.20% WACC by a massive 9.34 percentage points, the company is creating a very healthy Economic Value Added (EVA) spread. 

Ultimately, this heavily equity-funded model is a clear real-world example of the Pecking Order Theory in action. More importantly, it gives Bosch the financial breathing room to fund its massive pivot toward electric mobility and softwaredefined vehicles. By avoiding the heavy debt loads that trap others during industry slumps, Bosch has positioned itself to navigate the auto sector's inevitable cyclical downturns without taking on dangerous levels of financial risk.

title: A Neuroeconomic Analysis of Loot Box Regulation in the United Kingdom

detail.abstract: Despite generating over $15 billion globally in 2020, loot boxes are not legally classified as gambling under the Gambling Act 2005. The current framework only focuses on advertising and pre-purchase disclosures with no regulations regarding in-game mechanics. When left to self-regulate, the industry has demonstrably failed completely. A 2025 longitudinal study found that zero percent of games sought parental consent and only 8.6% consistently disclosed drop-rate probabilities.The obvious policy response to reclassify loot boxes as gambling is the wrong approach and the concerned authorities should instead use a mechanism-targeted approach. Loot boxes exploit a layered stack of neural mechanismsincluding tonic/phasic dopamine manipulation, insula suppression, salience engineering, OFC value inflation-which gambling regulations were not designed to combat. The primary audience for loot boxes is children whose prefrontal cortex (PFC) is structurally immature until the mid-twenties, rendering them measurably less able to resist these mechanisms when compared to adults. This paper suggests 3 policies: mandatory loss-streak counter to combat insula and LHb suppression, Verified parental consent via platform targeting the PFC developmental failure and independent statutory regulator with mandatory algorithm audit targeting the enforcement gap. When combined, these policies represent the minimum framework a mechanism-aware regulatory approach requires and a foundation for the DCMS and the Gambling Commission to build from in the next review cycle.

detail.abstract: Supply-chain management (SCM) research is analytically rich but representationally fragmented: studies are often identified by technology, method, industry, objective, or risk domain even when these descriptors refer to different aspects of the underlying managerial decision. This paper develops and evaluates the Supply Chain Decision Architecture (SCDA), which separates a four-dimensional Decision Kernel from Solution, Evidence, and Context layers. A reproducible review pipeline identified 705 unique candidate records; 659 advanced to Stage-2 screening and 518 were retained. A prespecified deep-review corpus contained 125 studies, including 121 primary analytical studies yielding 124 source-supported claims. Independent second-coder review showed heterogeneous agreement across the nine dimensions (Cohen’s κ = 0.036–0.712). Coder-sensitivity analysis nevertheless showed a consistent K4→KS7→KSV8→SCDA9 reduction in collision under both independent codings, although absolute collision levels differed substantially. Repeated 80/20 record-level holdouts further showed that preferred depth was coder- and sample-sensitive rather than universally fixed. In the frozen 124-claim analysis, collision decreased from 52.42% for K4 to 19.35% for KS7, 17.74% for KSV8, and 12.90% for SCDA9. The primary τ = 0.02 specification selected SCDA9, whereas a looser τ = 0.05 selected KSV8 and the original 24-study publication holdout selected KS7. A permutation diagnostic further showed that arbitrary independently permuted fields can reduce collision mechanically; collision is therefore interpreted only as within-corpus discriminability, not ontology validity. The evidence supports a layered decision-and-solution representation while treating outer-layer necessity as contingent on coding, sample composition, and analytical purpose.

detail.abstract: The Storage Location Assignment Problem (SLAP) is a fundamental challenge in warehouse operations, playing a crucial role in operational efficiency. It also directly influences order picking (OP), which alone accounts for a significant portion of total warehouse costs. While minimizing picker travel distance and time through data-driven strategies, such as correlated storage assignment, is common in the literature, these approaches often overlook high-density systems. Picker-to-parts warehouses that accommodate multiple products in the same location create bin heterogeneity, which is directly linked to intrabin searching time but frequently neglected in conventional SLAP studies. To address this gap, this research proposes a Multi-Objective framework for SLAP that jointly minimizes picker travel distance and time by maximizing item correlation, while reducing intralocation searching time by penalizing bin heterogeneity. The methodology uses historical order data and association-based methods to model item correlation, along with a tailored mixing index to address bin complexity. The resulting bi-objective storage optimization problem is solved using customized Multi-Objective Evolutionary Algorithms (MOEAs) and tested against different storage policies. This study distinguishes itself by leveraging real data from a footwear manufacturing company located in the province of Quebec, Canada, providing empirical evidence for practical solutions.

detail.abstract: Seniority-based wage systems coexist, uneasily, with the diffusion of performance-related pay, and firms that abandon seniority wages expose their youngest workers to a changed incentive environment. This paper reports three linked regression exercises carried out on synthetic data constructed to mirror an empirical study of these institutions: (i) a worker-level log-earnings equation estimated on 10,000 worker-year observations for 2,000 workers over 2016-2020; (ii) a firm-level logit for the adoption of performance pay estimated on 10,000 firm-year observations over 2020-2024; and (iii) a two-way fixed-effects difference-indifferences evaluation of a de-seniority reform introduced in 2019 by 250 of 500 firms, observed over 2015-2024. The entire analysis is implemented as a single scripted Stata workflow, from the import of the Excel workbooks through the export of publication-ready tables and figures. Every estimate recovers the parameter used to generate the data: the tenure return is 1.51% per year against a generating value of 1.5%; the performance-rating return is 8.35% against 8.0%; logit coefficients for export share, union density, and returns on assets fall 15-25% below the generating values, each within about two standard errors; and the reform reduces turnover of treated firms' under-35 workers by 2.16 percentage points against a generating value of 2.0, while leaving older workers unaffected. A pre-trend test does not reject parallel trends. Because the data are synthetic, these results validate the estimation pipeline, not the economics; they must not be cited as evidence on Japan's labour market or any real firm.

detail.abstract: Are state-owned enterprises (SOEs) worse, or better, than private firms once performance is measured on more than profitability? This paper compares 83 SOEs and 47 private firms listed in China on a five-pillar index of economic, technological, social, fiscal and long-term contribution built from CSMAR data. Comparing firms of similar size, leverage and industry over 2012-2024, the paper finds no systematic ownership gap: the SOE-private difference in the composite index is 0.003 standard deviations, and the 95% confidence interval excludes gaps larger than about 0.27. The result holds firm-level propensity score matching, inverse probability weighting and eleven alternative specifications of the index and the sample. SOEs tend to score higher on fiscal and social contribution and lower on technological effort, but none of these differences are significant at the 5% level, and an apparent improvement in the relative position of SOEs after 2017 is not robust. A second finding concerns measurement: results from an earlier version of the analysis, which normalised indicators within an inconsistent sector classification, compared scores built from different dimensions across years and treated repeated firm-years as independent in matching, do not survive once these problems are addressed. Comparisons of state-owned and private firms on composite measures should therefore report how normalisation and aggregation choices affect their results.

detail.abstract: Disclosing advisor affiliations is a widespread practice in early-stage fundraising, yet we know little about when such disclosures affect investor evaluations. To address this gap, we conduct a randomized field experiment embedded in the initial screening stage of a Singapore startup pitch competition. We independently vary the visibility of advisor affiliations, founding-team credentials, and market traction in standardized startup profiles shown to investors during initial screening. We find that advisor disclosure has its largest positive effect when foundingteam credentials are not disclosed, but it is far less able to compensate for undisclosed market traction. The effect of advisor disclosure is also stronger among less experienced investors and for B2B ventures. Our study provides causal evidence on advisor disclosure as a signal and shows that third-party affiliations are most valuable when they fill a specific informational gap.

detail.abstract: The diffusion of automation technology raises questions about the future of work, leading to calls for policy interventions. The ongoing debate centers on the decisions made by technology adopters. In this paper, I study supply-side adjustments and their role in shaping policy outcomes. I focus on the global market for industrial robots, a leading automation technology whose sales are dominated by a handful of multinationals. detail.abstract: Reflexive Resource Regulation (RRR) explains morality as the reflexive regulation of behavior across objective and social-resource conditions but the description begins only after a recognizable moralregulatory organization already exists. What it had not previously reconstructed in comparable detail was the evolutionary genealogy of that organization. The thesis advanced here develops a coevolutionary assembly account of how embodied moral-regulatory organization could emerge gradually from capacities that did not themselves originate as morality. The proposed sequence begins with separately evolved social capacities whose interaction alters relational environments. Those altered environments feed back into development and selection, while genetic, developmental, ecological, social, and eventually cultural forms of inheritance permit successful configurations to be repeatedly reconstructed. As social organization deepens, relations that initially confer advantages can become increasingly consequential to individual viability. Once access to protection, care, information, cooperation, reciprocal support, and other conditions of life becomes reliably mediated through relationships, a social being's own conduct can produce opposed consequences across objective and social-resource domains. Regulation must then become increasingly reflexive because the manner in which resources are acquired can preserve or damage the relational conditions through which future viability is sustained. The resulting embodied moral-regulatory organization provides the evolutionary substrate upon which later symbolic and explicitly normative forms of human morality can develop. The account integrates rather than replaces established work on social instincts, reciprocity, interdependence, niche construction, developmental inheritance, resource regulation, and symbolic cognition. Its distinctive contribution is to specify the organizational transition through which increasing relational interdependence can transform ordinary viability regulation into regulation of the self's effects upon the social conditions through which the self survives. The result is an understanding of the emergence of the evolved stress/eustress mechanism linking viability of the individual to group cohesion and cooperation. The essay introduces Path-dependent Relational Emergence Through Transgenerational Yoking: Key Interdependencies, Tradeoffs, Transmission, and Yield (PRETTY KITTY) formulation of evolutionary moral emergence as an extension Reflexive Resource Regulation (RRR) and the larger GTME project..

detail.abstract: This paper examines how foreign input-cost shocks transmit through domestic supply chains, shaping local economic vulnerabilities. Using detailed firm-to-firm domestic and foreign transaction data, we quantify the direct and indirect exposure of Italian labor markets to imports from China and from other extra-EU source markets. We assess the importance of firms' domestic and foreign sourcing linkages for overall exposure and highlight the critical role of wholesalers and top importing firms within the domestic network in shaping tail risks. Marked local disparities in exposure reveal that aggregate import statistics conceal substantial and uneven regional vulnerabilities.

detail.abstract: Accurate volatility forecasting is essential for the pricing and risk management of exotic interest rate derivatives. This paper presents a comparative analysis between econometrically driven GARCH-family specifications (GARCH(1,1), EGARCH, and GJR-GARCH) and non-parametric Implied Volatility Surface (IVS) calibration models in valuation framework for interest rate exotic structures, specifically Bermudan swaptions and ratchets. Utilizing daily yield curve data and swaption matrix quotes, we evaluate historical out-of-sample forecast accuracy, pricing residuals, and hedging error metrics. Our findings demonstrate that while GARCH models excel at capturing time-varying volatility clustering and fat-tailed residual distributions for short-term path dependencies, IVS calibration significantly outperforms GARCH-based pricing across cross-sectional exotic derivative payoffs by preserving the arbitrage-free static replication property. We highlight the operational trade-offs between dynamic time-series calibration and cross-sectional spatial surface parameterization, offering practical recommendations for quantitative risk management desk implementations.
