detail.abstract: Inspired by the recent development of perturbed-utility models, this paper revisits the traffic assignment problem through the lens of convex duality. It compares primal and dual representations of the shortestpath problem, the network-loading problem, and perturbed-utility traffic assignment in both link-path and link-node forms, and shows that they share a common structure in which Fenchel conjugacy links perturbation functions, surplus (or satisfaction) functions, choice probabilities, and network flows. In the cost-space dual, the gradient is the gap between the link flows supported by congestion and those demanded by network loading, so that equilibrium becomes a market-clearing condition with link costs playing the role of prices. Through this lens, a number of classical and recent formulations, including dual formulations of deterministic equilibrium, extremal formulations of stochastic equilibrium, logit loading algorithms that avoid path enumeration, and Markovian traffic equilibrium, emerge as variations of the same construction. The paper closes by discussing implications for the computation and estimation of network models, as well as a range of opportunities opened up by the perturbed-utility approach that remain to be explored.

detail.abstract: Schrepel and Jenny test whether a guidance text codifies practice that its authority's record already holds or announces policy in the voice of practice. They ran the test on a draft, which has no record after it. This paper builds the version of the test for a text with a history: each rule is followed across the versions of the text, dated by its first statement and read against a record on both sides of it, so that codification and announcement become dated events, rules practice has not yet reached are censored, and the legitimacy question moves to the texts that present their rules as practice. Run on five versions of the Swiss notice on vertical agreements (2002-2022) and two editions of its explanatory notes, against 2,527 Swiss decisions, it finds a notice that moved from announcing to codifying. The notices of 2002 and 2007 led practice (32 announcements against 8 codifications), and practice reached a rule not codified at its first statement a median 4.7 years later; the explanatory notes follow it (1 announcement among 31 norms), and a codified rule had been applied a median of at least 7.0 years before a text stated it. The notice, in which the statute empowers WEKO to set out the criteria it will apply, announces by design; the notes, which claim practice through their citations, pass, though the decisions they cite often hold only part of what they are cited for (49 of 116 pairs). The result holds under all five ways of combining the labels of two language models, given under a frozen protocol and checked against a human reader (Cohen's κ = 0.71).

detail.abstract: Commitment to producing impact is not enough: founders and other leaders of impact organizations should proceed only when the evidence supports both the proposed solution and an appropriate, sustainable form of organizational action. Before making substantial commitments, founders must undertake a disciplined five-part inquiry that defines the harm and unmet need, explains why the need persists, identifies a realistic opening for improvement, designs and tests a response and assesses whether that response can be delivered, financed and sustained. detail.abstract: The outbound investment channel has seen significant growth in the last three years as a number of factors enabled resident individuals to invest in foreign securities, property and funds, including the growth of the Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS), the retail-friendly offshore GIFT City International Financial Services Centre (IFSC), and the overseas exposure limit of domestic mutual funds that prompted retail and institutional investors to look beyond LRS. This report details the regulatory framework for outbound investment (LRS, Overseas Direct Investment/Overseas Portfolio Investment framework 2022 and GIFT City specific regulations), outlines the bottom up approach to arrive at the size of addressable market and profiles the competitive landscape in the segment of digital platforms, domestic mutual fund, GIFT City fund managers, private banks and independent wealth managers. While Traditional Retail Channel, the main channel of domestic mutual funds, has not been able to match its ceiling of USD 7 billion of overseas investment since 2022, Total LRS outward remittances have surged to USD 31.73 billion in FY2024 and are expected to slow down to USD 29.56 billion in FY2025, providing a structural opportunity for outbound MFs to be domiciled in GIFT City. The paper states that GIFT City is a policy relief valve, an exception to the SEBI cap, and that the competition is now bifurcating between the low cost digital platforms and the relationship-based wealth management platforms having offshore capacity in Dubai and Singapore for the high-net-worth and ultra-high-net-worth individuals. The regulatory environment is evolving rapidly, and there is no one official series of data on the flows of LRS by investment; many estimates in this paper are therefore presented as ranges and limitations in the data are clearly noted throughout.

detail.abstract: Generative AI now sits alongside leaders as they write proposals, position offerings, and plan campaigns, and it is often touted as a cure for biased decisions. This article argues that, when used without forethought, it can do the opposite: it can return a leader's own bias wrapped in the guise of polished, confident strategy. Based on two and a half years of practitioner observation across AI solutions firms and client organizations in Bangladesh, reported as anonymized composite vignettes, the article presents a five-stage Sycophancy Loop: loaded framing, curated context, agreeable output, override and capitulation, and velocity without verification. In high power distance cultures, where employees do not dare to challenge the boss, AI is often the only advisor able to disagree, yet it is trained to agree. To escape the loop, the article introduces the Executive Second Brain, five practices that transform AI from a mirror into a challenger: inquiry framing, constraint-grounded retrieval, a standing license to dissent, an override protocol with a dissent log, and a verification gate. It concludes with testable propositions and an actionable checklist for leaders.

title: What Happens When Countries Peg Their Exchange Rates?: The Real Side of Monetary Reform
affiliations: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management

detail.title: What Happens When Countries Peg Their Exchange Rates?: The Real Side of Monetary Reform

affiliations.org_name: Northwestern University - Kellogg School of Management

detail.abstract:
Many countries have adopted a fixed exchange regime in the context of a macroeconomic adjustment program in the hope of rapidly reducing their rate of inflation. Following the peg these economies tend to experience an increase in GDP, a large expansion of production in the non-tradable sector, a contraction in tradables production, a current account deterioration, an increase in the real wage, and a sharp appreciation in the relative price of non-tradables. There is a large literature that discusses the effects of the disinflation that follows the peg. This paper discusses a complementary channel of effects, associated with changes in the expected behavior of fiscal policy. A fixed exchange rate regime tends to be associated with an improvement, from the standpoint of the private sector, in the expected path of fiscal variables. Fiscal restraint is necessary to avoid speculative attacks against the currency; debt management has to be more careful; seignorage can no longer be used to finance increases in government spending before elections; and the more transparent costs of government activity provide an incentive to increase government efficiency.

In a simple small open economy model these fiscal impulses can help explain many of the symptoms experienced by economies that peg their exchange rate. This suggests that the real side of monetary reforms may play an important role in shaping the effects of fixed exchange rate experiences.

detail.abstract: Green supply chain management is a comprehensive approach that balances maximum profitability with minimizing environmental impact. This approach covers the entire supply chain (from raw material procurement to product recycling) by transforming a traditional supply chain into a green supply chain, enhancing organizational performance and increasing competitiveness. This study is developmental in terms of its purpose. The method employed for gathering data in this research involved conducting a systematic review. The collected sources included reputable articles related to green supply chain management keywords. The findings show that initially, 343 articles were identified based on the keywords; after filtering and closer examination, this number was reduced to ten articles. The results indicate that the successful implementation of green supply chain management not only reduces pollution and waste but also offers benefits such as improved brand image, reduced long-term costs, increased resource efficiency, and achieving a competitive advantage. Finally, strategies such as collaboration among supply chains, enhancing green supply chain management performance, and similar recommendations are provided. The main research question is: "What are the main variables in implementing green supply chain management?" Experts have examined and confirmed that these include process-related factors such as green design, green purchasing, and competition.

detail.abstract: Ceaseless technological innovations and regulatory policy changes have been fueling tectonic shifts in business environments, to which businesses sometimes resist via protests. While attracting public attention to the concerns they raise, the businesses protesting against another entity (i.e., a competing business or governmental institution) strive to make known the culpability of the external entity and garner support for the protesting business. Yet, three experiments show how the protesting business’ conflict with an external entity can trigger conflict between the protesting business and consumers. When such protests provoke perceived consumer victimization and antipathy toward the protesting business, consumers turn away from the protesting business and toward the competing entity—sometimes, ironically, the one that is being protested against. Such consumers’ antipathy toward the protesting business can be especially problematic for businesses relying on consumers’ purchase of their products and services. Importantly, the studies provide insights into how the political orientations of consumers can determine their response to business protests, as well as how protesting businesses can garner empathy and support by designing protest slogans that speak the political language of consumers who may be especially sensitive to the particular protest — i.e., protest slogans communicating liberal [conservative] values for business protests against changes brought about by governmental regulation [competing business]. The findings provide strategic guidance for businesses on ways to voice their concerns while incorporating the needs of various business stakeholders, promoting businesses to navigate the changing business environments constructively with the broader community.

detail.abstract: Online product reviews influence the choices people make while shopping. Customers often depend on ratings and written feedback before buying a product, but this system becomes unreliable when reviews are fake or intentionally misleading. Fake reviews may be posted to promote a product, harm a competitor, increase ratings, or create a false image of customer satisfaction. Detecting such reviews is challenging because fake reviews can look very similar to genuine ones. They may use realistic language, strong emotions, productrelated words, and believable experiences. For this reason, fake-review detection cannot depend only on sentiment or grammar. It may also require information about reviewer behaviour, review timing, rating patterns, text similarity, and possible coordination among reviewers. This paper reviews important research in fake-review and opinion-spam detection and proposes a practical machine-learning framework for future implementation. The framework includes dataset collection, data cleaning, text preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, prediction, explainability, human moderation, and continuous monitoring. It also discusses the use of classical machine-learning models, such as Naive Bayes, Logistic Regression, and Support Vector Machines, along with more advanced NLP approaches based on transformer models. The study is conceptual and based on existing literature. No new model has been trained or tested in this paper. Therefore, it does not claim a new accuracy score or experimental result. Instead, it presents an evaluation plan that can be used in future work, including precision, recall, F1-score, confusion matrix, inference time, robustness, and cross-dataset performance.

detail.abstract: The current study aims to increase engagement in community-driven content moderation by designing and testing simple, scalable interventions for social media platforms. We compare the effectiveness of interventions that increase awareness of the Community Notes initiative with collaborative booster interventions, which invite users to join Community Notes by asking a simple question about the initiative (Collaborative Inquiry), by emphasizing the role of human users in refining and rating notes initially drafted by AI (Collaborative Notes), or by repeating information about Community Notes (Notes Information). Using a 7-day longitudinal Instagram simulation study, we aim to show that the two collaborative intervention boosters will be more effective than merely increasing awareness of Community Notes in enhancing the likelihood of joining the initiative. In so doing, we help to promote a greater sense of shared reality among members of society, facilitating collaborative efforts to rebuild public trust and social stability.

detail.abstract: Massive digital transformation has prompted retail businesses to adopt omnichannel strategies as the primary approach in meeting the needs of modern consumers. But behind its various benefits, there is a dark side that has not been studied in depth, namely the phenomenon of negative immersion which has the potential to trigger a series of negative psychological reactions that lead to extreme customer churn behavior. This study specifically examines the psychological impact of negative immersion in the omnichannel ecosystem on customer churn intention, considering the mediating role of digital fatigue, cognitive overload, and customer disengagement in customer Rupa-Rupa.com in Manado City. A confirmatory quantitative approach was applied by involving 170 respondents who were selected through judgement sampling techniques. Data analysis was carried out using AMOS-based Structural Equation Modeling. The results of the study proved that all 16 hypotheses submitted received full empirical support without any of them being rejected. Negative immersion has been shown to significantly trigger digital fatigue, excessive cognitive load, engagement release, and customer churn intent. Customer disengagement was identified as the strongest predictor of churn intention as well as the most dominant mediator in the overall model of this study.

detail.abstract: Firms and researchers increasingly measure media coverage across text, images, and video, but estimating its causal effect on product demand is difficult because coverage responds to the very demand it may drive. We develop a framework that uses media outlets' editorial style to construct instruments for coverage, together with conditions and diagnostics that discipline their use. The topic-based Bartik instrument (TB-IV) interacts leave-one-out global topic flows with each outlet's predetermined topic shares, which must not predict local demand shocks. Grounding this requirement in the industrial organization of media markets, we derive three testable conditions (market separation, topic-share stability, and no spurious unit-specific trends) and characterize how exogenous topic-extraction error attenuates first-stage strength without invalidating the instrument. In a simulation built on real COVID-vaccine fact-checking texts, TB-IV yields accurate inference when its conditions hold, and a seven-step diagnostic checklist detects violations when they do not.

detail.abstract: The perception of a logo can be assessed not by opinions but by a measure: the psychological distance d from the sign to a reference. The article shows how quantified laws of psychology-those of Weber, Fechner and Stevens, signal detection theory, Thurstone, Shepard, the supernormal stimulus (Tinbergen), Rescorla-Wagner, Ernst-Banks, Luce, Hick, Fitts, the diffusion model, the forgetting and practice curves, the matching law, prospect theory, discounting, Sternberg, Spearman, Yerkes-Dodson, Zipf, Benford-can be read as functions of this distance and yield testable predictions: the detectability of a redesign, the transfer of a response from the reference to the sign, choice shares, and the speed and dynamics of memory. For each law an operationalization, a numerical example and a refutation condition are given. It is shown that the laws of discrimination, transfer and choice can be read as functions of one dimensionless quantity z = d / σ-the distance from the sign to the reference in units of noise: the form of the sign sets the numerator, the conditions of presentation set the denominator. The laws of channel, memory and sampling do not depend on z and set the conditions of measurement. The extensions-the field of signs (attentional priority, interference), demand and the owners' strategies-are built on the same two Euclidean quantities of MDS: d_k(S) to the reference and d_ij between signs. The asymmetry of similarity is described by a third measure, the Kullback-Leibler divergence over feature distributions, outside the base MDS. The reference is a pre-specified point, region or distribution in the same space as the sign; its content is not disclosed in the article, and the formal requirements for it reduce to fixing it before outcomes are observed and applying it identically to all signs. The article contains no empirical data: the numbers in it are illustrations, the predictions are hypotheses.

detail.abstract: Per-token AI prices keep falling, yet company AI bills keep rising. This paper reviews trade journalism, vendor pricing and documentation, consultancy analysis, and an academic study published between 2024 and 2026 to explain why. The findings show that cost is driven more by cost per task than by cost per token, and that a larger share of tokens does not necessarily mean a larger share of cost. The biggest change is the shift from tokenmaxxing to thrift-maxxing. This paper argues that optimizing token use beats simply cutting back, and that the real problem is the lack of a shared way to measure the value tokens produce. Without a standard, companies are managing AI costs guess by guess.

detail.abstract:
Introduction: In 2019, the 47 countries of the WHO African region (WAFR) lost a total of 50,396,061 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) due to particulate matter (PM) pollution. The study's specific objectives were to estimate the monetary value of DALYs and productivity losses (indirect costs attributable to particulate matter air pollution) per country in the WAFR.

Methods: The study covered all 47 WAFR member states and used the human capital approach (HCA) to value 50,396,061 DALYs lost at all ages due to particulate matter air pollution in 2019. A partial cost-of-illness method estimated potential productivity losses from 14,869,983 DALYs lost among adults aged 15 and older. Because the data covered a single year, the study was cross-sectional. Country-level analyses examined DALYs from six cause categories attributable to particulate matter pollution: acute lower respiratory infections; chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; ischaemic heart disease; stroke; tracheal, bronchial, and lung cancer; and other causes. We used Excel to analyse 2019 secondary data from the Institute for Health Metrics and Evaluation (DALYs), the World Health Organisation (current health expenditure per capita), the International Monetary Fund (GDP per capita), and the International Labour Organisation (labour force participation rates).

Results: Eliminating indoor and outdoor PM air pollution would prevent the loss of at least 50,396,061 DALYs, valued at Int$189,789,842,229 per year—equivalent to 3.8% of WAFR's total GDP in 2019. Interventions to eliminate indoor and outdoor PM air pollution would also save WAFR Int$33,573,411,191 annually in indirect costs (productivity losses), equivalent to 0.7% of its total GDP in 2019.

Conclusions: In 2019, particulate matter air pollution caused substantial health, welfare, and productivity losses in the WAFR. This economic evidence strengthens the case for multisectoral air quality control strategies and for more robust national health systems to manage diseases associated with particulate matter air pollution, recognising that health and healthcare are human rights for all WAFR inhabitants. To inform decision-making, further research in the WAFR is needed on economy-wide cost-benefit analyses of comprehensive air quality control strategies to mitigate the borderless adverse effects of all forms of air pollution on global climate systems, natural ecosystems, and human health.

detail.abstract: In an increasingly volatile, uncertain, complex, and ambiguous (VUCA) global environment, organizations face dual pressures to optimize existing operational capabilities while aggressively deploying digital innovations. This study investigates the structural mechanisms through which ambidextrous leadership drives sustainable organizational resilience via the mediating role of dynamic enterprise agility within emerging-market business enterprises. Anchored in the Dynamic Capabilities Framework and the Resource-Based View (RBV), we posit a structural model examining exploratory and exploitative leadership behaviors, process agility, market responsiveness, and multifaceted resilience (operational, financial, and strategic). Employing a cross-sectional, quantitative survey design, empirical data were gathered from N=412 senior executives, general managers, and chief technology officers across technology-enabled, manufacturing, and financial services firms in India. Structural Equation Modeling via Partial Least Squares (PLS-SEM) was utilized to test the hypothesized paths and mediation effects. The results demonstrate that ambidextrous leadership exerts a statistically significant positive effect on organizational resilience (=0.342,p<0.001) and enterprise agility (=0.584,p<0.001). Furthermore, enterprise agility significantly mediates the relationship between ambidextrous leadership and organizational resilience (=0.286,p<0.001), accounting for a substantial indirect effect. The findings provide practical and theoretical frameworks for enterprise leaders navigating digital transformations under UGC-CARE and global research benchmark criteria, highlighting that structural ambidexterity without dynamic process adaptation yields suboptimal long-term stability.

detail.abstract: Can AI assistance help workers produce legal work that meets a quality benchmark within a restricted working-time allowance? I reanalyze public data from an experiment assigning 153 law students to three complete sequences of unaided work, Vincent AI and o1-preview across six legal tasks. I reproduce average improvements in quality and reported time use, then examine a joint indicator requiring five recorded quality scores averaging at least 5 and reported time no greater than 75% of the task budget. Across all 918 scheduled participant-task observations, the recorded qualifying rate is 14.38% without AI, 23.20% with Vincent and 29.41% with o1-preview. Task-adjusted differences are 8.82 and 15.03 percentage points, with participant-clustered 95% intervals of [3.34, 14.30] and [9.27, 20.79]. Threshold and task-composition analyses clarify where these gains occur. An audit also shows that unrestricted task-specific coefficients in the public participant-fixed-effects interaction model are not uniquely identified, although average contrasts are estimable. Worst-case bounds for underlying qualifying performance cross zero because some outcomes are incompletely recorded. The results provide evidence about documented performance under an illustrative joint benchmark and show how measurement and sequence assignment shape the interpretation of AI productivity experiments.

detail.title: UK Data Protection After Brexit: Between the EU and the Most Developed Commonwealth States?

affiliations.org_name: University of Cambridge - Faculty of Law

detail.abstract: Although the UK retained an EU-derived legal model of data protection post-Brexit, in September 2021 its Conservative Government launched a non-radical initiative for the primary law reform of this which was extensively influenced by legislation in the other most economically developed Commonwealth States (namely, Australia, Canada, New Zealand and Singapore). This ultimately led to the Data (Use and Access) Act (DUAA) 2025 under the subsequent Labour Government. However, with very partial exceptions related especially to the partial restriction of solely automated decision-making rights, none of the proposed reforms to core data protection duties which were influenced by most developed Commonwealth experience-including any formal move to a more risk-based accountability framework-were adopted. DUAA therefore fell short here even of the Digital Omnibus proposals now put forward by the EU itself. In contrast, most of the similarly-influenced proposals concerning regulation were adopted including a statutory controller-led complaints process and new Data Protection Authority (DPA) obligations related to promoting trust and confidence, innovation and competition and safeguarding public and national security. Regulatory convergence with these other jurisdictions is undergirded by wider changes including the UK DPA's own rejection of regular and strong use of its formally formidable dissuasive sanctioning powers. Considering both cogent criticism of the unrealistic and unreasonable nature of many EU data protection duties and a growing recognition (including in Australia and Canada) that strong enforcement is crucial to ensuring trustworthiness and the rule of law, it is questionable whether this highly asymmetric learning is normatively appealing.

title: How Knowledge Crosses Borders: Evidence from Semiconductor Manufacturing
affiliations: Yale University - Department of Economics, University of British Columbia (UBC), Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and University of Georgia

detail.title: How Knowledge Crosses Borders: Evidence from Semiconductor Manufacturing

affiliations.org_name: Bureau for Research and Economic Analysis of Development (BREAD)
Government of the United States of America - Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System

detail.abstract: We show that cross-border learning is an important feature of modern semiconductor manufacturing and that several important channels – such as knowledge sharing along global supply chains, the movement of engineers within multinational firms, and foreign direct investment – operate through market mechanisms rather than anonymous technological spillovers. These findings have significant policy implications. When cross-border learning is mediated by purposeful economic relationships, access to frontier knowledge is neither automatic nor guaranteed. Firms and governments can facilitate – or restrict – the international diffusion of technology, implying that policies to foster domestic technological upgrading are likely to be most effective when coupled with continued access to global sources of frontier knowledge.

detail.abstract: Does direct integration into native schools or temporary placement in separate schools better promote the education and cultural assimilation of refugee children? In the Netherlands, primary-school-aged refugee children are placed in either integrated or separated schools depending on their randomly assigned municipality. By contrast, all secondary-school-aged arrivals are initially separated. We exploit this institutional setting in two-way fixed-effects models with age-at-arrival and municipality fixed effects. Using rich administrative data, we find that integrated schooling reduces educational attainment at age 18, particularly for children of lower-educated parents. At the same time, integrated schooling increases cultural assimilation, measured by hormonal-contraceptive usage among teenage women, particularly for children from non-Muslim-majority countries. A distinctive feature of separated schooling that may account for its positive educational effect is that it allows employing teachers specialized in native-language teaching for non-native speakers.

title: Do Agricultural Price Shocks Persist? A Fractional Integration Analysis for the MENA Agricultural Markets
affiliations: Brunel University London - Department of Economics and Finance, University of Navarra - Department of Economics and Federal University of Technology Akure (FUTA)

detail.title: Do Agricultural Price Shocks Persist? A Fractional Integration Analysis for the MENA Agricultural Markets

affiliations.org_name: Brunel University London - Brunel Business School
CESifo (Center for Economic Studies and Ifo Institute)
German Institute for Economic Research (DIW Berlin)

detail.abstract: This study investigates the persistence and mean-reversion properties of major agricultural commodity prices in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region using a fractional integration framework. The analysis focuses on wheat, rice, maize, sugar, and soybeans under alternative specifications for the error process, including white-noise, Bloomfield autocorrelated, and seasonal autoregressive errors. The results are found to depend critically on the specification of the disturbances. Under white-noise and seasonal autoregressive errors, the estimated fractional differencing parameters exceed one for all commodities, indicating strong persistence and providing little evidence of mean reversion. However, allowing for autocorrelation as in the Bloomfield specification lowers the estimates below unity for all commodities. Significant mean reversion is found for wheat, rice, and soybeans in the case of the original series, while only soybeans exhibit significant mean reversion in the case of the logged series. Thus, agricultural price shocks do not all have permanent effects: their persistence varies across commodities and depends on the underlying error structure. These findings have implications for strategic reserves, agricultural trade, food-price stabilization, and food-security policies in the MENA region.

title: Platform Liability, Product Safety and Optimal Pricing
affiliations: University of Bielefeld, Bielefeld University - Department of Business Administration and Economics and University of Hamburg - Department of Economics

detail.title: Platform Liability, Product Safety and Optimal Pricing

affiliations.org_name: Bielefeld University - Department of Business Administration and Economics
University of Hamburg - Department of Economics

detail.abstract: Should platforms be held legally responsible for harm caused by products or services offered by third-party sellers? We address this question in a novel setting in which product safety (the likelihood of accidents) is determined by third-party sellers, while the consumer price is set by a monopolistic platform that pays sellers a commission. Relevant examples include platforms providing ride-hailing services (e.g. Uber and Lyft) or health care services (e.g. Teladoc). Sellers decide whether or not to become active on the platform, and consumers' willingness to pay for the platform good increases with the number of active sellers (platform externality). When an accident occurs, the harm is divided between the platform and the respective seller according to a liability rule set ex ante by a welfare-maximizing policymaker. Sellers' incentive to provide high product safety is driven by market demand, which in turn is determined by the platform's pricing scheme, balancing the trade-off between market revenue and expected liability costs. The platform may optimally set a price below the monopoly level to boost demand, thereby triggering active sellers to provide high product safety (market channel). The socially optimal liability rule is dichotomous: it either assigns no liability to the platform, or the maximum liability share for which the platform exploits the market channel to induce high product safety from the sellers. Holding the platform liable is socially desirable only when it induces lower consumer prices.

title: Everyone Is a Manager: AI Use as an Act of Management
affiliations: Cornell University - Cornell SC Johnson College of Business and Monash University

detail.title: Everyone Is a Manager: AI Use as an Act of Management

affiliations.org_name: Cornell University - Cornell SC Johnson College of Business
Cornell University - Charles H. Dyson School of Applied Economics and Management

detail.abstract: When a knowledge worker is given an AI assistant, they stop executing tasks and start delegating them. Thus, we propose that the use of AI is an act of management, which helps explain the heterogeneity in returns to AI use observed across firms. We model the return to AI as moderated by two managerial abilities: direction (how well the worker specifies what they delegate) and verification (how reliably they catch the tool's errors). As AI becomes more reliable, the skill with the higher marginal return shifts from verification to direction. To the extent that use builds skill, workers develop their managerial abilities in the normal course of work, but as the tool improves, direction will continue to build while verification will not. As increasingly fewer tasks are worth checking, the skill collapses. Workers will reach that point sooner if they only bear part of the cost of their errors. In equilibrium, the strongest verifiers tend to sort into the jobs where collapse is most costly.
